en: The Explanation of the Words:
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Having paid homage to the Buddha-lotus, the vessel of the honey of the True Dhamma,
The wise teacher Moggallāyana composed this concise and easy-to-understand treatise on phonology (*saddalakkhaṇa*),
which is adorned with strings of qualities and frequented by the honey-bees of the Saṅgha.
I shall begin, in brief, this manual for the accomplishment of words for the benefit of the ignorant—
the *Paddhati* (Guide) to the jewel-mine of the meanings of the *Moggallāyana-Śabdārtha*; herein, by means of the analysis of grammatical designations (*saññā*),
the vowels and other elements are treated according to their defining characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*).
I shall first demonstrate that very [system] through its divisions, showing how they are known:
there are forty-three vowels, beginning with *a*.
According to the words of the Victor, the consonants (*akkhara*), ending with the nasal *niggahita*, are forty-three; each of these is called a "vowel" (*vaṇṇa*).
For example: *a ā i ī u ū e o ka kha ga gha ṅa ca cha ja jha ña ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa ta tha da dha na pa pha ba bha ma ya ra la va sa ha ḷa aṃ*.

Here, the letter *ka* and so forth have the letter *i* (*i-kāra*) for the purpose of pronunciation; the meaning is "that by which [something] is articulated" (*vaṇṇīyati*), thus they are called *vaṇṇā* (articulants). Those beginning with *a* are the *a-ādayo*, being delimited by *a* and so forth.

The term "beginning with *a*" (*ādayo*) continues [to apply] as far as "the nasalized *bindu*. This is a transformation of case endings (*vibhattipariṇāmo*) based on the sense of the word. It is connected with the locative ending (*sattamyanta*), as in "among those beginning with *a*.

The vowels beginning with *a* and ending with *o* are designated as the ten sounds; these ten vowels—namely *a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, e, o*—are called "vowels" (*sarā*) because they flow or proceed (*saranti pavattanti*). The phrase "the ten, beginning with *d*" (*dasā do*) continues throughout the three sections being recited.
Two by two, they are of the same class (*savaṇṇā*).

Among the vowels (*aāsvādimesu*), those two by two are called "of the same class. According to their respective order—namely, *a* and *ā*, *u* and *ū*, *e* and *o*—these are "similar" (*samānā*) or "identical" (*sādisā*) letters, being of the same class (*savaṇṇā*). This state of being the same is due to their place of articulation (*ṭhānato*).
For there are six places of origin for the letters: the throat, palate, lips, teeth, nose, and the chest. Among these, [the letters] *avaṇṇa* (the *a*-vowels), the *ka*-group (*kavagga*), and *ha*...
The throat is the place of origin for the *i*-vowels and the *ca*-group; the palate for the *ṭa*-group and the *ra*-vowel;

the head for the *ta*-group and the *la*-vowel; the teeth for the *u*-vowels and the *pa*-group; the lips for the *e*-vowel; the throat and palate for the *o*-vowel; the throat and lips for the *va*-vowel; the teeth and lips for the *niggahīta*;
and the nose for the *ṅa*, *ña*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *ma* sounds. The phrase "each respective place" and "both" carry over [from the previous rule].
Among those ten vowels, each pair consists of two of the same color; whichever is the first in each pair is designated as short—namely *a*, *i*, *u*, *e*, and *o*.
Among these, those preceded by a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) are also seen; however, the last two are shown there for the sake of illustrating their excellence.
Here, *saṅgaha* (grouping) refers to the short vowels due to their brevity, or because they possess that quality; likewise for the long vowels.

Here too, the phrase "two by two" applies. That which follows [a short vowel] is long. Among the ten vowels beginning with *ā*, those which are paired as homogeneous sounds (*savaṇṇa*), each subsequent one is designated as "long"—namely: *ā, ī, ū*.
The consonants are *kādayo*.
Among the vowels beginning with *a*, the thirty-three letters starting with *ka* and ending with *niggahīta* (the anusvāra) are called consonants (*byañjana*), as follows:
ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa; ca, cha, ja, jha, ña; ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ṇa; ta, tha, da, dha, na; pa, pha, ba, bha, ma; ya, ra, la, va, sa.
*Ha*, *ḷa*, and *aṃ*: "Meaning (*attha*) is manifested (*byañjīyati*) by these" is the definition of *byañjana*; thus, the consonants beginning with *ka* are what is being discussed.
There are five groups (*vaggā*) of five [consonants] each.

Among those beginning with *ka*, the five sets starting with *ka* and ending with *ma* are called "groups" (*vaggā*), namely: *ka-kha-ga-gha-ṅa*, *ca-cha-ja-jha-ña*, *ṭa-ṭha-ḍa-ḍha-ṇa*, *ta-tha-dha-dha-na*, and *pa-pha-bha-bha-ma*. They are called "groups" (*vaggā*) because they "exclude" (*vajjenti*) the letters beginning with *ya*.

The *bindu* (dot), which is the nasal sound following vowels such as *a* and others, that consists of a single *bindu*, is designated by the technical term *niggahita*. That which is grasped and uttered in dependence upon a short vowel is *niggahīta*. This is the formulation of the technical designation (*saññā-vidhāna*).

"Sandhi" refers to the following: *purisuttamo* (the supreme man), *paññindriyaṃ* (the faculty of wisdom), *satārakkho* (protected by mindfulness), *bhogindo* (lord of enjoyments), *cakkhāyatanaṃ* (the eye-base), *abhibhāyatanaṃ* (the base of mastery), *dhanamme atthi* (I have wealth), and *kuto ettha* (whence here?). In these cases, there is the elision of a vowel before another vowel (*sare lopo sare*).

A vowel is subject to elision when followed by a vowel (*sare*). This occurs in a locative case of proximity (*upasilesikādhārasattamī*); therefore, the grammatical operation does not take place when there is an intervention by a consonant or time—such as in *tvam asi* (you are) or *katamā cānanda aniccasaññā* (and what, Ānanda, is the perception of impermanence?). Furthermore, this proximity-based locative case is also applied in other instances where [vowels] are joined together.
When "the seventh case ending is prescribed" is being stated:
"In the seventh case, [the suffix] follows the preceding word.
Since it is prescribed that the suffix follows the preceding word in the description of the seventh case, there is elision of the preceding vowel: *purisuttamo*, *paññindriyaṃ*, *satārakkho*.
Bhogindo, the sense-base of the eye (*cakkhāyatana*). The sense-sphere of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*), there is wealth, where is this?
Because the seventh case is indicated by the performance of the preceding operation, "subsequent-ness" (*paratā*) is understood;

thus even the expression "after that" (*paretu-parivacana*) is appropriate—[as in] "I am he," "these four," "from which water," "early in the morning," and "thus here"—wherein the rule "elision of *sa* before a vowel" (*saro lopo sare*) applies.
A vowel after another vowel is sometimes to be elided: *sohaṃ*, *cattārome*, *yatodakaṃ*. And before *tu*: [Is it] always? No. For example: *paññindriyaṃ*.
The rule for *assa* applies in all compound junctions (*sandhi*): *tassidaṃ*, *tassidaṃ*, *vāteritaṃ*, *vāteritaṃ*, *sītodakaṃ*, *sītodakaṃ*.
Regarding *udakaṃ*, *vāma ūru*, and *vāma ūru*: after the elision of the preceding vowel (*itidha-pubbasara-lope*), the rule "or when a vowel follows" (*sare veti*) also applies.

When a consonant (*ñ*) follows a semi-vowel (*yuvaṇaṇaṃ*), there is elision (*lutta*). After an elided vowel followed by a vowel, the *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels optionally become *ñ* respectively, according to their order.

“By the word *vaṇṇa* (color/sound), even that which has the same sound (*savaṇṇa*) is included. Because the word *vaṇṇa* follows [the previous rule], it includes even those with the same sound; and because of this, *ī* and *ū* are also included as substitutes for *e* and *o*. This is [an example of] *tassidaṃ* or *tassidaṃ-vāteritaṃ*. *Vāteritaṃ* means cold water (*sītodaka*). By the rule “when a consonant follows, the long vowel is used,” it becomes *sītudakaṃ*. *Vāmoru* (beautiful-thighed) is from *vāmūru*, where the *u* is elided. What are these ten?

*Vaṇṇaparena savaṇṇepi.* *Vaṇṇasaddo paro yasmā tena savaṇṇopi gayhati sayaṃ ceti ī ū nampi e o-tassedaṃ, tassidaṃ-vāteritaṃ.* *Vātiritaṃ-sītodakaṃ, “byañjane dīgarassā”ti dīghe-sītudakaṃ-vāmoru, vāmūru-luttetikiṃ-dasa ime.*
Because the word *kvaci* (in some cases), which prevents over-extension, follows [the previous rule], the prescription of an alternative (*vikappa*) is not fixed;
therefore, in such instances as *upeto*, neither the alternative nor the prescription regarding *nāraka*, etc., occurs. Thus: *ci akāsi, ci akāsi*.
"Su āgataṃ, su āgataṃ"—here the rule *ve* from "of the vowels *e* and *o*" continues to apply.

When a vowel (*sara*) precedes and another vowel follows, the letters *y* and *v* optionally arise in place of the vowels *ṇ*, *u*, and *vaṇ*, respectively. For example: *Akārassa dīghe*: *vyākāsi*. *Yāgame*: *vanataragāvā gāmā* (with the augment *viyākāsi*). *Svāgataṃ*, *Sāgataṃ*, *kvacitveva*, *yānīdha*.
*Te ajja*, *te ajja*, *so ayaṃ*, *so ayaṃ*. In this context, the rule "when a vowel precedes" (*yavāsare*) and the particle "optionally" (*ve*) are understood to apply.
In each instance, the letters *y* and *v* respectively become [the corresponding semivowels] when followed by a vowel; for example:
*tyajja*, *tejja*—[this occurs] by the rule “long vowels become short before consonants”—thus: *svāyam*, *soyam*.
In some cases, the phrase “*go eḷakam itidha sare*” is supplied [from a previous rule]. When a vowel (*sara*) follows, *avaṅ* is the substitute for *go*.
This occurs when there is the possibility of the entire word being replaced by the rule “*ṭ-anubandhāneka-vaṇṇa-asabbassā*,” while the term “*antasse*” is being supplied [from the current context].

[Objection: But surely it is a *bandha* (suffix). That which has the letter *ṅa* as its *anubandha* would thus have more than one phoneme at the end; therefore, it applies only to the vowel *au*. [Response: Because of the statement, “A *saṅketa* (conventional designation) is a non-component *anubandha*,” there is no application of the letter *ṅa*. Its purpose is that the conventional designation “*ṅ-anubandha*” serves as a marker (*gaveḷaka*).
Thus indeed, thus indeed—“*tīdha-*.”
When the word *eva* follows the word *iti*, the form *vo* optionally replaces *itissa*;
this applies when [the pronoun] ends in the genitive case.

Whatever grammatical operation (*kāriya*) is prescribed for the sixth case (*chaṭṭhi*), that should be understood as applying to the final [sound] of that [base]; thus, there is a substitution (*ādesa*) of the vowel *i*.

[This is because] "the substitute (*ādesa*) is seen—that is, pronounced—in place of those [sounds] which are subject to elision (*āmaddiya*)," with the exception of the *y*-substitution. For instance, by the rule "for the *ta*-group and *va-ra-ṇa*, there are the *ca*-group and *ba-ya*" (*tavaggavaraṇanaṃ ye cavaggabayañā*), the letter *t* becomes *v*;
and by the rule "for those [consonants] following the *va*-group and *la*," the letter *y* becomes *c*. Thus, in the word *ajja* (today), having changed *ci* to *itvā*, it becomes *ajja*.
*Agge*, *pātu*, *ahesuṃ*, *pā*, *eva*, *idha*, *ijjhati*, *pari*, *antaṃ*, *atta*, *atthamiti*—hereafter, the term *maya-dā-sare* applies.
Furthermore, *vata-tara-gā* are *āgamas*.

These *maya-dā* or *āgamas* optionally occur before a vowel (*sare*) in certain instances; even when there is no fixed rule for the *āgama*, it is the vowel itself that becomes the *āgama*, as in *vanādinaṃ tu*.
The prescription of grammatical rules (*yuk*) for words and so forth by means other than those that indicate [the rule] is purposeless; it consists of two parts:

having piled up [the examples], such as *ajjatagge* and *pāturahesuṃ*, [one says] "in the case of a short vowel when there is a long vowel in the consonant," and even before that, [there is] *idhamijjhati*, *pariyantaṃ*, *attadatthaṃ*, and *vātveva-attatthaṃ*.
There are six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), six direct knowledges; here, the phrase "or an augment (*āgama*) occurs after a vowel" also applies.
Chā ḷo.
The letter ḷ becomes an augment (āgama) optionally after the word *cha* before a following vowel: *chaḷabhiññā*, *chaabhiññā*.
Vowel-sandhi.
In the case of *kaññā iva* (like a girl), when the elision of both the preceding and the following sounds would apply, the rule "the vowel remains" (*saro paro*) also applies.
Or it may not: in some instances, both the preceding and the following sounds are optionally not elided—thus: *kaññāiva*, *kaññeva*, or *kaññāva*.
The prohibition of the *sarasandhi* [euphonic junction] therein:
"Delight in that, patience is supreme; it has been rightly proclaimed"—here, in the case of *byañchane*, the vowels are long and short.

In certain instances, long vowels become short when followed by a consonant; therein lies delight. Regarding the phrase "khantīparamaṃ, sammadaakkhāto," the vowel is short according to the traditional scripture (*āgama*). In the rule "kvaci ītve ca tyajja," as in the example "yāniva antalikkhe," the terms "long" and "short" are established through the division of grammatical rules (*yogavibhāga*).

The letter *ci* denotes the third meditative absorption (*jhāna*). The letter *vi* denotes a hiatus (*khopa*). Here, the phrase "itidha byañjane" continues to apply. From a vowel, two [consonants] follow.
In some cases, two forms of another consonant arise through *saramhā* (elision of a vowel):

the compound (*viggaha*) form, and when [the preceding vowel] is followed by fourth or second [consonants], the third and first [of those respective groups] arise. When followed by other fourth or second [consonants], the third and first of those same groups arise in place of the fourth and second [consonants] respectively, provided they belong to that same class (*tabbagga*), according to the rule of "subsequent truth" (*paccāsatthi*).
The third jhāna consists of the letters *ja* and *ka* among the *pubba-jhakāra* and *khakāra* [groups]; "distraction is from the vowel"—what is that?
It is the word *taṃ vanaṃ*. Regarding *akarambhasete*, *akarambhasete*: this is the meaning, this is the meaning;
thus, the phrase *iti dha ce* follows. [In the rule] *e o na ma vaṇṇe*.
And in some cases, when there is no *vā* or *a* following the consonant, as in *akaramha sete*, the meaning is *eso attho*; "in the case of *vaṇṇe*"—what is the example?—it is *so*.

This is the combination of vowels and consonants (*sarabyañjanasandhi*). Examples include: *ata yantaṃ*, *tatha yaṃ*, *mada yaṃ*, *budhi yati*, *dhana yaṃ*, *seva yo*, *payesanā*, *pokkharaṇa yo*; thus it is here.

The *tavagga* (the *ta*-group) and *varaṇaṃ* (the *naṃ*) [become] the *cavagga* (the *ca*-group) and *khayaṃ* (the *yaṃ*), respectively. The *tavagga* and *varaṇaṃ* become the *cavagga* and *bayaṃ* respectively before the letter *ya*:

according to the rule “*vaggalasehi te*,” the *vaggas* [become] the single substitute for the preceding form of a following *ya*. Examples: *tacchaṃ*, *majjaṃ*, *bujjhati*, *dhaññaṃ*, *sebbo*, *payyesanā*.
The term *pokkharañño* occurs in some instances; the word *matyā* continues [as a governing rule] for the three [suffixes] about to be mentioned:
*saka*, *yate*, *ruca*, *yate*, *paṭyate*, *lupyate*, *salyate*, and *disyate*; here, [the suffix] *te* follows after [roots ending in] the labial (*vagga*) or *la*.
In certain instances, the gutturals (vaggā) and laterals (lasā) of another [word] become gutturals and laterals [themselves].

For example: *sakkate*, *ruccate*, *paṭṭate*, *luppate*, *sallate*, *dissate*. In some cases only—namely in the case of *kyāhaṃmuha* [becoming] *yatī’tīdha*—there is a substitution (*vipallāsa*) of the letter *h*.
There is a substitution of *ha* for *ya*, as in "yakāro-muyhati" (the letter *ya* is forgotten).

In the phrase "bahuābādho, bahu ābādho" found here in the *ussavakāra* (the festive/celebratory section), the expression "substitution of *ha*" (*hassa vipallāso*) applies. This is the *vevā* (etymological analysis).
The perversion of hatred occurs. In the word *bahvābādho*, it is *bahv-ābādho*. This is a euphonic combination (*byañjana-sandhi*).
[The term] “the eye aches” (*akkhirujati*)—here, the particle *iti* is understood to apply as far as the phrase “in my dwelling” (*mayadāsare*).
*Niggahitaṃ*.

Regarding the statement *niggahītamāgamo hoti vā kvaci* (“the *niggahīta* becomes an augment in some cases”), it means that [the *niggahīta*] goes by embracing its substitute (*ṭhānin*) and proceeds [into the following sound].

Thus, in examples such as *akkhiṃ rujati* and *akkhi rujati*, because the governing rule (*adhikāra*) is established as either permanent (*nicca*) or optional (*vibhāsā*) from the beginning [of the section] by the phrase *yāvadvidhā*, the word *vā* (or) is used.

Indeed, [the particle] *hi* occurs in two senses: in some cases it expresses an alternative (*vikappa*), and in others it denotes the grasping of a form as it has been defined (*yathāvavatthitarūpapariggaha*).
When it occurs in the latter sense, it indicates a positive injunction (*vidhi*) regarding that which is impermanent and non-existent.

Here, however, because the word *kva ci* (in some cases) follows, the injunction of non-existence is established by that very [particle]. Thus, in the word *saṃramho*, there are two forms—*saṃramho* and *saṃramho*—which are masculine (*puṃliṅga*). Masculine...
Regarding the term *liṅgam*: here, under the heading of the *niggahīta* (the nasal stop), there is the rule "ā mayadā sare" [Kacc 149].

This is an elision (*lopa*). There is optionally an elision of the *niggahīta* in certain instances where long vowels follow, as in *sāramho*, *sāramho*, *pulliṅgaṃ*, *puṃliṅgaṃ*, *paṭisallāṇe pātukāmo*, and so forth. Also, in cases such as *pupphaṃ assā*, *pupphaṃ assā*, *kiṃ iti*, and *kiṃ itī*. Here—
Regarding *parassa*:
there is optionally the elision of a following *sa* after a *niggahīta* in some instances. There is also the elision of the first member of a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*).
"An immediate consonant [is elided], or there is sometimes the elision of that which is the first member of a conjunct. Thus, there is the elision of the *sassādissa* (the final *s* with its vowel):

*pupphaṃsā*. By the rule "mayadā sare," the *niggahīta* becomes *m*: *pupphamassā*. By the rule "in a class [of consonants], the final of the class [is substituted]," the *niggahīta* becomes *k*: *kinti*, *kimiti*.

At that moment, at that moment, one should practice the Dhamma; one should practice the Dhamma. That burns, that burns. That is the gift, that is the gift. That is the fruit. That is *elamiti* here—at the end of the section in the section.
For one who has grasped [the word], there is either the end of the section in the section, or "paccāsatyā," "taṅkaṇaṃ," "taṃkhaṇaṃ," "dhammañcare."
"One who practices the Dhamma is diligent; being diligent, he is free from sloth; being free from sloth, he attains its fruit;

having attained that fruit, he is called 'one who has gone' (gata)"—in such passages as these, they speak of what is "constant" and "immediate" (*ānantarika*); they speak of what is "immediate," which is indeed personal (*paccattaṃ eva*), for that is indeed so.
Thus, in this world, it is truly empty.
For indeed, in the case of words, there is either the substitution of *ñ* for the *niggahīta*, according to the rule “*vaggalasehi te*” (by those of the same class or *l* and *s*).
One should not say that this applies when there is an immediate following *ñ*. That which is called "immediate" (*ānantarika*) refers specifically to the doubling of *ñ*;
it is indeed specific to that, as in *taṃhi eva* and *saddasahacariyāya*. Thus, only the word *ya* is taken here—as in *saṃyato, saṃyato*.
Whatever *niggahīta* occurs after *saṃ* or *saṃsa*, that becomes *ña* before the letter *ya*.
In *saññato* and *saṃyato*, only the mere presence of the letter *ya* is intended, because of the repetition [of the rule].
*Tam eva, tam eva, tam idam, tam idam, tam iminā, tam iminā* [occur] before a vowel in *mayadā-sare*.
In some cases, the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) optionally becomes *maya* before a vowel: *tameva*, *taṃeva*, *tayidam*, *taṃidam*, *tadaminā*.

In this context, by the rule “*tadaminādīni*,” the letter *i* is replaced by *a*. By this same rule, all instances of elision (*lopa*), augmentation (*āgama*), and transposition (*vipallāsa*) not prescribed by other specific rules are to be understood.

Thus, forms such as *nijako* and *niyako* are established. In cases such as *buddham saraṇam iccha*, the separation of the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*) applies. This concludes the section on the euphonic combination of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra).
Now, the names are being stated.

They are of various kinds according to their gender (liṅga) and number (vacana). Among these, first regarding those ending in the vowel *a* in the masculine gender (*pulliṅga*), when the word *buddha* is followed by the seven case endings (*vibhattiyo*), it stands as follows:
*buddho*. From a noun (*nāmasmā*), for the singular and plural [of the nominative], there are *si*, *yo*, *nā*, *hi*, *naṃ*, *smā*, *sanaṃ*, *smiṃ*, *su*.

"Of these [two], there are two [forms] each, because they function in both singular and plural senses; thus, according to the sequence, when the singular is to be expressed from a noun (*nāma*), the singular endings are used, and when the plural is to be expressed, the plural endings are used—this is the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for the application of suffixes.

In the mere sense of the nominative (*paṭhamātthamatte*), there are the meanings of the base (*sakattha*), substance (*dabbā*), gender (*liṅga*), number (*saṅkhā*), and the five beginning with the object (*kamma*)."
The meaning of "name" (nāma) is said to be merely its commonality.

When there is the mere requirement for an expression of a name, the nominative case occurs; thus, by the power of the speaker's intention, there are the nominative singular and plural endings. *Si* is the nominative suffix;

the purpose of the letter *s* being an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) is its connection with the *tap-paccaya* (nominal suffix). An example of this convention is: “kiṃ maṃ sīsū” (what is my head?). Thus [it is explained].

The rule *aṃ vacanassakārassa si ato* continues [from the previous sutta]. Since that [term] is a qualifier of the noun (*nāmavisesana*), by the principle *vidhibbisesanantassa*, the operation applies to that which ends in it.
Thus, *sissa*.
After a noun ending in the vowel *a*, the suffix *si* becomes *o*; there is elision of the preceding vowel (*pubbasaralopa*). *Buddho tiṭṭhati*—[the suffix] *yo* [is applied].

Hence, *ṭā* and *ṭe* are substituted for the nominative (*paṭhamā*) and accusative (*dutiyā*) case endings following a noun ending in the letter *a*. Because the letter *ṭ* is an *anubandha*, the rule “*ṭanubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbassā*” applies, resulting in a replacement of the entire word-form. Thus: *buddhā tiṭṭhanti*. The phrase “in the sense of the nominative alone” (*paṭhamātthamatte*) continues to apply. [Now follows:
In addressing (*āmantaṇe*).
"The first case ending occurs for the mere sense of address when there is an existing object to be addressed, such as 'There is no king,' which brings about presence through sound;
in this [instance], the singular number is used for a single entity. Thus, *si* is the singular.
In the case of *gosyālapaṇe*:
"In *ālapaṇe*, *ga* is designated as *sañña*; [the rule] 'there is elision' (*lopo*) applies. [This refers to] *gasīnaṃ*.
The elision (*lopa*) of *asmi* does not occur after *āgasīnaṃ*. [Examples: *bho buddha maṃ pālaya* (O Buddha, protect me);

*ge* (in the word *ge*). Alternatively, there is lengthening (*dīgha*). [Rule: In the case of these [words], lengthening optionally occurs when followed by *ge*, according to the rule "lengthening in all three genders. Thus: *buddhā* (O Buddhas). Some desire lengthening only for calling from afar; however, since it is seen even in calling from nearby, that [restriction] should not be accepted. [Examples: *yo’mhi* (I who am), *buddhā maṃ pāletha* (O Buddhas, protect me).
The Objective Case: The factor of action connected with the agent and the act is called the object (*kamma*);
it is threefold, being distinguished as that which is produced, that which is transformed, and that which is attained.

The word *matikaññā* is the same [in form]. Thus, for the word *timsa* (thirty) and its derivatives such as *timsati*, the forms are identical.

Furthermore, regarding *silope* (elision of *si*), due to the analysis of the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*) "long and short," there is also the form *tiṃsa* with the elision of the nasal (*niggahīta-āgama*) in the short vowel;
likewise, in the subsequent cases as applicable, for the forms beginning with *dvattiṃsati*, there are *dvattiṃsa*, *dvattiṃsā*, and *dvattiṃsanti*.
Similarly, for the forty: *cattāri*, *cattāḷīsā*, *cattāḷīsa*, and *cattāḷīsaṃ*; likewise, *cattārīsā*, *cattārisa*, and *cattārīsaṃ*.
And for *dvi* [the following applies]: when *asatāda*, *anaññattha*, and *cattāḷīsa* follow, *dvi* optionally becomes *dvissa* or *ā*; thus:
*dvecattāḷīsa*, *dvācattāḷīsa*, *dvīcattāḷīsa*, likewise *dvevattārisa*, *dvācattārīsa*, *dvicattārīsa*, *dvecattāḷīsati*, *dvācattāḷīsati*, *dvicattāḷīsati*.
Forty-four, etc.
When *asatāda* does not have another meaning, there are the forms *catālīsādo*, *tissa*, or *tecattālīsa*, *tivattālīsa*, *tecattālīsati*,
*ticattālīsati*, *tecattārīsa*, *ticattārīsa*, *dvipaññāsa*, *dvāpaññāsa*, *dvepaññāsa*, *dvepaññāsati*.
Fifty, sixty-two, sixty-two, sixty-two; sixty-three, sixty-three; seventy-two, seventy-two, seventy-two, seventy, seventy-two, seventy-two;
seventy-three, seventy-three, seventy-three, seventy-three;
eighty-two, eighty-two, eighty-two—here the augment *y* occurs—eighty-three, eighty-three; ninety-two, ninety-two, ninety-two.

Ninety-nine hundred (9,900); the neuter singular forms are thus: thousand and so forth—ten million (koṭi), ten billion (pakoṭi), one hundred billion (koṭippakoṭi), and one trillion (akkhobhiṇī)—these are feminine singular forms.
However, in the division of groups, all numbers indeed take the plural;
for example: two twenties, three twenties, and so forth. Ten hundreds is called a "thousand" (sahassa). Ten thousands is a "ten-thousand" (dasasata).
A thousand, ten thousand, a *nahuta*, ten *nahutas* is a *lakkha*; a hundred thousand is also called a *lakkha*.
A hundred *lakkhas* is a *koṭi*; a hundred thousand *koṭis* is a *pakoṭi*; a hundred thousand *pakoṭis* is a *koṭippakoṭi*. In this manner:
a *nahuta*, a *ninnahuta*, an *akkhobhinī*, a *bindu*, an *abbuda*, a *nirabbuda*, an *ahakaha*, an *ababa*, an *aṭaṭa*, a *sogandhika*, an *uppala*, a *kumuda*.
The *puṇḍarīka*, *paduma*, *kathā*, and *mahākathā* should be understood as having successively one hundred thousand times the merit of the preceding one.
Now, the "incalculable" (*asaṅkhyeyya*) is explained.
It is of two kinds, according to the division of *pādi* and so forth. In this regard: *pa*, *ra*, *a*, *pa*, *saṃ*, *anu*, *ava*, *o*, *ni*, *du*, *vi*, *adhi*, *api*, *ati*.
Furthermore, *su*, *u*, *abhi*, *pati*, *pari*, *upa*, *ā*, *ime*, *vīsati*, *pādayo*, *cādayo*, *pana*, *ca*, *vā*, *ha*, *aha*, *eva*, *evam*, and so forth—

these two types [of particles] are devoid of gender and number; however, by means of these, all case endings (*vibhatti*) prescribed according to possibility [are applied], and in the case of those without number (*asaṅkhyehi*), [all case endings are applied].
For all other case endings (vibhatti), there is elision (lopa) because they are non-existent [in this context].
From that, the distinction of case endings occurs for nouns with gender (saliṅga); likewise, for the words *tumha* and so on, there is no such thing among those without gender (*aliṅga*).
Those ending in *syādi* have thus been explained.

Now, the meaning of *ekattha* (synthesis) is stated: after the prefix *upa*, the nominative singular suffix *-si* is elided by the rule “*asaṅkhyehi sabbāsaṃ*. From the word *kumbha*, the genitive singular suffix is applied, resulting in *kuma-as*.

At this stage, according to the rule “*aviggaho niccasamāso padantaraviggaho ve*” (a compound is always a non-analysis; it is an analysis of separate words), there is an analysis of separate words (*padantaraviggaha*) such that [the prefix] is near the jar (*kumbha*).
Then, by the rule “*syādi syādinekatthan*” (words ending in case-suffixes are used with words ending in case-suffixes in a single sense), it functions everywhere as a single sense (*ekattha*).

*Asaṅkhyam*: An indeclinable (*asaṅkhya*) ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*), when occurring in the sense of distribution (*vibhatti*), proximity (*sampatti*), vicinity (*samīpa*), totality (*sākalya*), absence (*āhāva*), according to order (*yathāpacchā*), or simultaneity (*yugapad*), becomes a single syntactical unit (*ekattha*) with another word ending in a case-suffix. This is the state of being a single syntactical unit (*ekatthatā*). 1. *Vibhatti* (Distribution): *Paṭipāṭiyā paṭipāṭiyā ti paṭipāṭikaṃ.* (One by one, in succession, thus "successively. 2. *Sampatti* (Success/Prosperity):

*Sukhaṃ sukhanti sukhasukhaṃ.* (Happiness, happiness—thus "continuous happiness. 3. *Samīpa* (Vicinity): *Gāmaṃ gāmanti gāmāgāmaṃ.* (Village after village—thus "from village to village. 4. *Sākalya* (Totality): *Sabbaṃ sabbaṃ ti sabbasabbaṃ.* (All, all—thus "entirely all. 5. *Āhāva* (Absence/Exclusion): *Na na ti nānā.* (Not, not—thus "variously" or "not at all. 6. *Yathāpacchā* (According to Order): *Purimaṃ purimaṃ ti purimapurimaṃ.* (The first, the first—thus "each preceding one. 7. *Yugapad* (Simultaneity): *Ekakkhaṇe ekakkhaṇeti ekakkhaṇekakkhaṇaṃ.* (At one moment, at one moment—thus "simultaneously. In these cases, the indeclinable ending in a case-suffix forms a compound with the other word ending in a case-suffix. This is called *ekatthatā*.

In compounds such as *īya-ādi*, when there is a state of unity (*ekatthibhāva*), that is "unity" (*ekatthatā*); therein, the elision of the *syādi* suffixes occurs. Because it is neuter according to the rule “*taṃ napuṃsakan”* (that [compound] is neuter), the *syādi* suffixes are subject to elision by the rule “*pubbasmāmādito*” (elision after the preceding *am*). [The rule:
“*Nāto mapañcamiyā*” (there is no [elision] of the fifth case ending after *am*). After a preceding word in unity that ends in *a*, there is no elision of any of the case endings following it.
There is *aṃ* [as a suffix] after the fifth case (*pañcamī*) [ending]. *Upakumbhaṃ tiṭṭhati*: "he stands near the jar"; the meaning is "he stands in the vicinity of the jar.

Or, [the suffix *aṃ* occurs] after the third (*tatiyā*) and seventh (*sattamī*) cases. When a compound (*ekattha*) ending in *a* precedes, there is optionally *aṃ* after the following third and seventh case endings: *upakumbhaṃ*.

It is said: *upakumbhena*, or *kumbham upa*, *dehi pañcamiyam amabhāvā upakumbhā*, *apehi upakumbham*, *upakumbham āyattam*, *upakumbham nidhehi*, *upakumbhe vā*—and likewise *upanagaram* and so forth.
Regarding proximity (*samīpam*), [the rule] "from the beginning of *pubba* onwards" applies to all cases where the initial [syllable] is elided;
thus it is applied everywhere, as in *upagurum* and so on.

Amādi. A word ending in a case-suffix (syādyanta) frequently forms a compound (ekattha) with another word ending in a case-suffix: *gāmaṃ gato* becomes *gāmagato* ("gone to the village"), and *muhuttaṃ sukhaṃ* becomes *muhuttasukhaṃ* ("momentary happiness"). This is indeed the function of the *upapada* [rule].

In the case of *māse kumbhakāro* ("a potter working in the month"), here, by virtue of the rule concerning "frequently" (*bahula*), it is also combined with a word ending in a case-suffix that begins with *a*.
Compound (samāsa). Hearing the dharma with those ending in -nta, -māna, or -ktavantu: *dhammaṃ suṇanto*, *dhammaṃ suṇamāno*; having eaten rice: *odanaṃ bhuttavā*;
struck by the king: *raññā hato rājahato*; pierced by a sword: *asinā jinno asicchinno*; like the father: *pitarā sadiso pitusadiso*; food mixed with curds:

*dadhinā upasittaṃ bhojanaṃ dadhibhojanaṃ*; rice mixed with sugar: *guḷena misso odano guḷodano*. In these cases, however, the formation occurs through the very word (*pada*) itself, such as "mixed" (*upasitta*) and so forth.
Because it expresses an action, there is no lack of connection with its own meaning; in some cases it is merely a suffix, as in *uraga* (snake);

in some cases it is merely a compound, as in *erasunā chinnava* (cut by a sickle), *dassanena pahātabbā* (to be abandoned by seeing), *brāhmaṇassa deyyaṃ* (what is to be given to a brahmin) which becomes *brāhmaṇadeyyaṃ*, and *yūpāya dāru* (wood for a sacrificial post) which becomes *yūpadāru*.

Here, however, there is no [suffix], as in *saṅghassa dātabbaṃ* (to be given to the Saṅgha). In the case of *gāmā niggato* (gone out from the village), it becomes *gāmaniggato*; in some cases it is merely a suffix, as in *kammajaṃ* (born of karma). Here [it is likewise].
A man fallen from a tree is not a royal official (*rājapurisa*), because of the great authority of the king’s officials;

[this is] for the purpose of excluding those who are highly honored. It exists in the sense of "becoming" (*bhavati*); it is not "imitating me," nor is it "acting like me. Among cows, the black one is the most abundant in milk; among pupils, the fifth;
the whiteness of a cloth—[these examples show that] the present tense indeed exists in certain cases to express proximity to the action (*vattamānasāmīpya*), as in "the fruits are ripe."

In the phrase *phalānaṃ suhito*, [the genitive] is with respect to the fruit (*phala*); in *brāhmaṇassa kaṇhā dantā*, it is with respect to the teeth (*danta*). Here, because there is no relationship [of the genitive] with *kaṇha*, there is no compound.

For a compound occurs when there is a mutual relationship [between the members]. However, when it is an attributive compound (*visesanamāsa*) such as "those which are black and are teeth" (*kaṇhā ca te dantā ca*), then the genitive is with respect to the black teeth;
thus it indeed becomes *brāhmaṇakaṇhadantā*. In the phrase *rañño māgadhassa dhanaṃ*, [the genitive is with respect to the king].
In the term *rañño*, the genitive case (*chaṭṭhī*) expects wealth (*dhana*); it is not the case that "the King of Magadha" (*māgadharājā*) is expressed by the word *māgadha* alone.

Because there is no distinction [between the two meanings], there is no relationship [of dependence]. Thus, the word *rājā* is not compounded with *māgadha*, which shares the same grammatical locus (*tulyādhikaraṇa*).

In the expression *rañño asso ca puriso ca* ("the king’s horse and the man"), because each is related separately and thus possesses expectancy (*sāpekkhatā*), there is no compound; [for example,] *asso*.
When the compound *rājapuruṣa* (king’s man) is formed as a *catutthi-samāsa* (dative compound), it remains exactly as *rājassa puriso*.

However, in the case of *rañño garuputto* (the king’s heavy son), although it depends on the word "king" (*rājāpekkhino*), a compound is still formed with the son of the heavy person because it is intelligible (*gamakattā*). Intelligibility is also a basis for compounding;

thus, *dānasoṇḍo* (greedy for giving) is a compound where the suffix is applied after the word "giving" (*dāne soṇḍo*). In some instances there is simply a grammatical function (*vutti*); for example, *pabbataṭṭho* (standing on the mountain). In certain compounds, even when a case-ending is elided (*vibhatyalopo*), the word remains intelligible, such as *janesuto* (heard among people).

Regarding the rule for *ekattha* (coalescence) with an adjective (*visesana*): An adjective ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*) becomes *ekattha* with another word ending in a case-suffix that has the same referent (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

For example, "that which is blue and it is a lotus" (*nīlañca taṃ uppalañca*) results in the compound *niluppalaṃ*. In the original sentence, the use of the word *ca* ("and") is for the purpose of indicating the state of having a common referent; however, in the grammatical derivation (*vutti*), [it is omitted].

Because it is explained by means of a compound (*samāsa*), it is not merely its application [that is intended]; this is stated elsewhere as well because of the predominance of the rule regarding non-application (*appayoga*) in the places where it has been mentioned.

In some instances, a qualifying term (*visesana*) that serves as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) comes after [the noun it qualifies], as in *sīho ca sīho muni ca so sīho ca* = "the sage is a lion and he is a lion," thus *munisīho*.

Alternatively, the word *muni* alone is the qualifier; for when "lion" (*sīha*) is uttered, there arises a general understanding of both metaphorical and non-metaphorical lions, and the word *muni* [serves to specify].
It qualifies [the term]: *sīladhanam* means "virtue as wealth. *Dhammasammato* means "one who is honored for the Dhamma," being one who is honored as the Dhamma.

When the compound *mahatī ca sā saddhā ca* (and that faith is great) is formed, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is absent due to the rule “*itthiyam bhāsitapumitthi pumevekattha*” (in the feminine, when a word has been stated as masculine, it remains masculine in a single referent). Then, by the rule “*ṭantantunanti ntassa ṭe*,” the *nt* is replaced by *ṭ*.
Finally, by the rule “*byañjane dīgharassā*,” the vowel is lengthened, resulting in *mahāsaddhā*.
*Ñañ*.

This term *ñañ* may end in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*) and forms a compound (*ekattha*) with another word ending in a case-suffix. The letter *ñ* is for the purpose of specification (*visesanattha*), so that [the rule] does not apply in cases such as *pāmanaputtādi*.
[The example is: *ṭanaññassa*.

The suffix *ṭa* is substituted for the word *nañ* when it occurs before a following word (*uttarapada*). For example: *na brāhmaṇo* = *abrāhmaṇo*. This *nañ* functions both as a *pariyudāsa* (exclusionary negation) and as a *paṭisedha* (prohibitive negation).

In the first case (*pariyudāsa*), one understands that a person other than a Brāhmaṇa—such as a Kṣatriya or others who do not aspire to be Brāhmaṇas—is indeed similar to a Brāhmaṇa, yet is called "non-Brāhmaṇa" (*abrāhmaṇa*).
In the second case (*paṭisedha*), however, due to some cause for doubt regarding a Kṣatriya or similar person...
In the case of the word *brāhmaṇa* when it is flowing [as a suffix], the cessation of false knowledge (*micchāñāṇa*) is effected;
the meaning is that there is no "brahmin" in what is not a brahmin, nor is there an absorption (*ajjhāsita*) in being a brahmin.

In that context, because false knowledge can arise even without similarity, and due to the capacity of the grammatical operation (*payoga*), there occurs a treatment as if there were similarity, and the gender and number belong to that [original base]. For this very reason, it is said:
In a compound where the negative particle *nañ* is connected [to the following word] and the sense is similar to that of *maññati*, there is likewise a connection with the meaning;

thus, in this way, the predominance of the meaning of the first member of the compound remains even when the suffix *-añ* is added—such as in *anasso*. Here, [the rule applies] before a vowel (*a-sare*).
When *uttarapada* (a following word) follows, the word *nañ* becomes *ana*; thus, for *na*, there is *ana*.
Words beginning with *ku-* are always [used] in the context of rules concerning *as-*, etc.

The word *ku-* and those beginning with *pa-* form a single meaning (*ekattha*) with a word ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*), always in a sense other than that which falls under the scope of rules concerning *as-*, etc., when it denotes something contemptible (*kucchita*).
*Brāhmaṇo* becomes *kubrāhmaṇo*; *evaṃkupuriso* [becomes *evampakupuriso*]; in the sense of "or a man" (*purise vā*), there is the substitution of *ka-* for *pakkha-*;

*kāpuriso* [becomes *kapuriso*]; *īsakaṃ uṇhaṃ* becomes *kaduṇhaṃ*—here, by the rule “*sare kada kussuttaratthe*,” there is the substitution of *kada-* for *kussa-*; *appakaṃ lavaṇaṃ* becomes *kālavaṇaṃ*—here, by the rule “*kāppatthe*,” there is the substitution of *kā-* [for *appa-*].
In the case of words such as *pāda* used in the sense of "gone to," etc., the nominative case is employed.
The teacher has gone; the student has likewise [gone]. "Well-done" means done well; "ill-done" means done with difficulty.
Words such as *accanta* (excessive) take the second case in the sense of "extreme" (*kantādya*) and so forth.
*Atimāla* means one who has gone beyond the garland.
In the case of *ghapa*, *ssānta*, *appakāna*, *antabhūta*, and *appadhāna*, when followed by *ghapa* or words beginning with *sya*, there is shortening; thus, [the vowel] is shortened.
In *ava-vāda* and so forth, the third case is used in the sense of "walls" (*kuṭṭha*) and similar meanings.
*Avakokilaṃ* means a forest abandoned by cuckoos; *avakuṭṭhaṃ* means relinquished.
In the sense of "overpowering," such as in the case of illness and so forth, the fourth case ending (*catutthī*) is used.
*Pariyajjhena* means the act of overpowering for the sake of devouring.
The suffixes *nya* and so forth occur after a word ending in the fifth case (ablative) in the sense of "departed from" (*nikkanta*) and so on.
In the compound *nikkosambi*, formed with *gha* and other suffixes, the [final vowel] is shortened. Or, in the sense of "not one" (*nekañña*), [the suffix *ya* occurs].
In the sense of a word ending in a case-suffix (*syanta*), there may be a single compound meaning for multiple words: *otiṇṇo haṃso yam so* becomes *otiṇṇahaṃso* (a lake where a swan has descended);
*jito māro yena so* becomes *jitamāro* (the Blessed One by whom Māra was conquered); *chinno taru yena so* becomes *chinnataru* (the axe by which the tree was cut);
*dinno suṅko yassaso* becomes *dinnasuṅko* (the king to whom tax was given); *apagataṃ kālakaṃ yasmā so* becomes *apagatakālako* (the cloth from which blackness has departed); *pahutaṃ dhanaṃ*.
When the compound is formed as "one who has cows that are incomparable" (*asamā*), where the word *yassa* [is the relative pronoun], there is no one equal to that wealthy man;
for *yassa*, there is the substitution of *ṭā* [for the final vowel], and it is followed by *gāvo*. [In the genitive plural] *gossu*.

In the case of words such as *go* (cow), when it is at the end of a compound and not followed by *appa* or *dhana*, the substitution of *u* occurs for the final vowel before suffixes such as *-ī*. For example: *cittagu-* (possessing a mind), *gomā* (possessing cows). The term *mattānekagajaṃ* (a forest with many intoxicated elephants) refers to that [forest] in which there are many intoxicated elephants.
*Saputto* (accompanied by a son) means existing together with a son, or "with a son.

According to the rule *“sahassa so’ññatthe”* (the substitute *so* is used for *saha* when expressing other meanings), in the alternative analysis (*viggahe*)—namely, “he who is with a thousand”—it is analyzed as: *dhavā ca badirā ca palāsā ca* (the Dhava, Badira, and Palāsa trees).
In the sense of a compound (catthe). Several words ending in case-terminations may become a single meaning (ekattha); namely, there are four types of compounds:

collective (samuccaya), distributive (anvācaya), mutual conjunction (itarītarayoga), and aggregation (samāhāra). Among these, the state of becoming a single meaning (ekatthībhāva) is possible for the words in both mutual conjunction and aggregation.
Because there is no mutual relationship [between the members], it is not a conjunction (*samuccaya*), nor is it a secondary addition (*anvācaya*), since those [conditions] are absent;
thus, the word *ca* is excluded.

In the case of a collective compound (*samāhāra*), the neuter gender applies. When there is a unification of meaning in a collective sense, that takes the neuter gender—since the collective itself is a single entity, it takes only the singular number—as in: *dhavakhadirapalāsaṃ katthaṃ* (a bundle of Dhava, Khadira, and Palāśa wood).

Regarding the phrase *ci na hoti ‘asabhāparisā’*: it is an indicator [of the rule]. In a compound consisting of a governing head and its attendants (*ādhipacca-parivāra*) joined together (*itara-itara-yoga*), the plural number is used because the members [of the group] are predominant, as in *dhava-khadira-palāsā*.
In a compound, that which was mentioned first is placed first; since there is no purpose for deviating from the sequence, [the order is maintained].
However, in some cases, there is an inversion due to the general rule of "frequently" (*bahula-adhikārato*), such as *rājadanta* (king-tooth), meaning "the king of the teeth. [The term] *pāpa*...

In the compound *bhūmiyasmiṃ pāpā ca sā bhūmi ca*, having analyzed it as such, the rule governing the final member of a compound applies. [The suffix] *a* is added to the end of a compound whose latter member is *bhūmi* following words such as *pāpa*.

Thus, when *bhūmi* follows *pāpa* and so forth, the suffix *a* is applied to the end of that compound: *pāpabhūmaṃ* (a place). By the rule beginning with *itthiyaṃ*, etc., the feminine suffix *āp* is excluded; since the ground (*bhūmi*) is characterized by its genus (*jāti*), it is called *jātibhūmaṃ*.

"Count them, count them! Regarding the stage that follows: "having two stages" (*dvībhūma*) means it has two stages; likewise for "three stages" (*tibhūma*) and "four stages" (*catubhūma*). Due to the predominance of the plural form, in some instances the singular is not used, as in "four stages.
[The compound] *dīghāho* is formed with *aho*, *vassa*, and *ekadesa*, and [the feminine form] *ratyā*.
After the words *dīgha* and so forth, as well as after numerals (*saṅkhya*), the word *ratti* becomes *ra* when compounded with another word in the sense of non-otherness (*anañña*).
Being a compound ending in *ra*, it becomes *a*: *dīghā ca sā ratti ca* → *dīgharattaṃ*; *ahaśca ratti ca* → *ahorattaṃ*.

Because the word *aha* (day) begins with *a*, [the rule] "for *man* and those beginning with *a*, *o* is substituted for *vassāsu*" applies, resulting in *vassārattaṃ*. Furthermore, *pubbā ca sā ratti*...

The term *atī* is used with *pubbarattaṃ* (the first part of the night) and likewise with *apararattaṃ* (the latter part of the night). When the middle of the night (*aḍḍharattaṃ*) has passed, it is called *rattiṃ atiratto*.

*Dvirattaṃ* is a compound of two nights (*dvinnam rattīnam samāhāro*). The suffixes *-dīgha*, *-ratti*, and *-uparatti* occur only after numerals that do not signify "another" (*anañña-saṅkhyatthesu eva*), because of the rule of frequent application (*bahulaṃ vidhānā*); for example, *yathārattaṃ*.

The word *go* becomes *gava* in a compound ending in *alopa*, provided it does not signify "cow" (*cattha*). When the word *go* occurs at the end of a compound with elision (*alopa*), it becomes *gava* before the neuter suffix *a*, unless the compound signifies "cow" (*cattha*) or refers to something other than a number (*asaṅkhyatta*).
For example: *rājño go rājagavo* (the cow of the king); *pañca gāvo dhanam assa* (five cows are his wealth). Here, *avaṅ* replaces the vowel.

The compound *pañcagavadhana* is an *aññapadattha-samāsa* (compound whose meaning is other than its constituent members) containing within it a *visesana-samāsa* (attributive compound). In the case of *dasagavaṃ*, which is a *samāhāra-samāsa* (collective compound) meaning "a collection of ten cows," why is there elision (*alopa*)?

[Answer: Because of the rule "purchased with five cows" (*pañcabhir gobhiḥ krītaḥ*), which is an *aññapadattha-samāsa*. By the rule "formed by that" (*tena kṛtam krītam*), etc., the suffix *ṇika* is applied; when there is elision of that [suffix] by the rule "elision" (*lopa*), and the suffix *kan* is added, the vowel *u* in the word *go* is replaced by *ava* by the rule "in the state of being" (*avasthā*).

Why is this so? [Counter-example: *ajassa gāvo* ("the cows of the goat")—here, because the number is not other [than one], the suffix *yu* is applied only in the sense of "belonging to" (*tassa idaṃ*). Thus, *cittagu*.
In the compound *upaguvisālāni akkhīni assa* ("whose eyes are large like those of an ox"), the suffix *a* is applied by the rule *akkhismāññatthe*.

Regarding this, some say that there are four types of unity (*ekatta*) and three types [of duality] based on the predominance of the sense of the subordinate member (*aññapadatthata*). Others will explain later that unity is fourfold—namely, "prior" (*pubba*), "subsequent" (*uttara*), "both" (*ubhaya*), and "other" (*aññattha*)—while duality is threefold, distinguished by the sense of both members (*ubhayatthatā*).
This is one point.
Now, those [words] ending in feminine suffixes are explained. [The suffix] *am* occurs when expressing femininity.
The suffix *āp* occurs after feminine nouns ending in the vowel *a*: *devadattā*, *ajā*, *kokilā*, and so forth. After [nouns] beginning with *nadī*, the suffix *ṅī* occurs.

This belongs to the class beginning with *ā*—that is, the suffix *ṅī* occurs after words beginning with *nadī* in the feminine sense; the letter *ṅ* [is for the purpose of indicating that] "in the case of *ṅī*, the *t* of *nta* and *tu* becomes *to*" (Pāṇini 7.1.80).
The conventional meanings are: *nadī*, *mahī*, *kumārī*, *taruṇī*, *vāruṇī*, *gotamī*. Regarding the word *gacchantī*:

by the rule “*ntantūnaṃ ṅimhi to ve*” (the *t* of words ending in *-nt* or *-tu* becomes *ī* before the feminine suffix *ṅī*), there is the form *gacchatī*; likewise *guṇavantī* and *guṇavatī*—for these are read among the *nadādi* group by the rule “*gotovā*” (the *t* of *go* optionally becomes *ī* before *ṅī*).
Or, by the rule “*gossāvaṅ*” (the word *go* takes the suffix *āvaṅ* before *ṅī*), there is *gāvī*, [and] *go*.
And [the suffix] *nī* is applied after a feminine word ending in *yakkha*.
A woman who is possessed by a *yakkha* becomes *yakkhinī* (by adding *nī*) or *yakkhī*; likewise *nāginī* or *nāgī*. [The suffix] *nī* is also applied after words ending in *yu* and *vaṇṇa*.
The suffix *nī* occurs frequently after words ending in *vaṇṇa* when denoting a woman: *payatapāṇinī*, *daṇḍinī*, *bhikkhunī*, *paracittavidunī*.
From the word *yuvan*, the suffix *tī* occurs in the feminine: *yuvatī*.
[The suffixes] ending in *itthi* and *paccaya*.
Now, the [suffixes] beginning with *ṇa* are stated: in the analysis (*viggahe*) of *raghussa apaccaṃ*, [the rule] *ṇe vāpacce* [applies].

From a noun ending in the sixth case (the genitive), the suffix *ṇa* occurs when the meaning is "fit for" (*hotabba*). The letter *ṇ* is an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) for the purpose of applying the rule of *ṇa*-suffixes; since the meaning "fit for" is already expressed by the suffix itself, the word *apacca* is not employed [in the compound]. Due to "identity of referent" (*ekatthatā*), there is the elision of the case endings and so forth.

Regarding the rule "for vowels, after the first [vowel], *ā*, *u*, and *i* become *ē*, *ō*, and *ō* respectively when followed by a suffix with *ṇ* as an *anubandha*": among the vowels, those beginning with the first vowel (*a*)—namely the vowels *a*, *i*, and *u*—become *ā*, *ē*, and *ō* respectively when followed by a suffix with *ṇ* as an *anubandha*. Thus, for the vowel *a*, it becomes *ā*.
Regarding the rule *uvaṇṇassa avaṅ sare sarādo ṇanubandhe*:

because of the prescription that the *uvaṇṇa* [vowels *u*, *ū*, *uṇ*, *uṃ*, *uḷ*] becomes *avaṅ* before a vowel when followed by a suffix beginning with *ṇ*, such as *syādi* (the case endings), *rāghavoccādi* (words like *rāghava*), or in the feminine, *rāghavaccādi* (words like *rāghavī*), it follows that from *raghu* there arise both *raghupacca* and *ragvapacca*.
Furthermore, words ending in *ṇa* and so forth take the gender of the object denoted (*abhidheyyaliṅga*), but in the sense of "descendant" (*apacca*), they are neuter.
In the neuter gender, when expressing a collective sense, the suffix *ṇya* is added,
as well as the forms derived from *bhāva* and *samūha*; furthermore, in the sense of satisfaction or enumeration,
words ending in suffixes such as *tva* and others are used in the neuter gender, or sometimes in the masculine.
"Niddissati" (he will point out) refers to when the specific details of what is to be known have been selected.
Or, "vā" (or) indicates an alternative application.
From "vaccha" and so on, the suffixes are "ṇa", "ṇaya", and "nā".

The suffixes *-pacca*, *-ṇa*, and *-ṇaya* are added after [names] such as *Vaccha* to form patronymics (*gotta*) and the like, beginning with the great-grandson (*paputta*). For example: from *Vaccha*, *Vacchassa pacco* becomes *Vacchāno*;

*Vacchāyano*. Because it is stated that "there is no vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*) when a conjunct follows," there is no strengthening; thus, from *Kattiya*, *Kattissa pacco* becomes *Kaccāno*; *Kaccāyano*.
When forms preceded by the letter *y* or the *c*-group follow, the augment *y* is inserted, resulting in *Kātiyāno*.

In compounds such as *kattikāya apaccam* (the day after the full moon of Kattika), the suffixes *-ṇeya* and *-ṇera* are applied after words beginning with *kattikā* and after words beginning with *vidhavā*, respectively.

That is to say, after words beginning with *kattikā* and after words beginning with *vidhavā*, the suffixes *-ṇeya* and *-ṇera* occur in their respective order, as in: *paccekattikeyyo*, *veṇateyyo*, *vedhaverō*, and *sāmaṇero*.

The suffix *ṇya* is optionally applied after words beginning with *dis* (direction) and so forth, as well as after *diti* and its derivatives, when followed by *gotra* or a patronymic (*paccaya*). In some instances,
it is also applied after a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*).

In the case of those vowels beginning with *a* that serve as bases for suffixes, *ā*, *e*, and *o* sometimes become [the substitutes] when a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) follows; this is because the locative case is indicated by the word "in the domain" (*visaye*). Since it is specified in the locative, the vowel *e* occurs before the cluster. There is elision (*lopa*) of *avaṇṇa* and *ivaṇṇa* vowels before an affix beginning with *ya*.

There is elision of *avaṇṇa* and *ivaṇṇa* vowels before an affix beginning with *ya*: the offspring of *Devī* is *Decco*; the offspring of *Kuṇḍanī* is *Koṇḍañño*. There is the prior form (*pubbarūpa*) of *na* before *ñe*: the offspring of a brother (*bhātuno*) is *Bhātabbo*. Here—
In a suffix beginning with *y*, there is *avaṅ* for both *go* and *suvaṇṇa*. Thus, *avaṅ* replaces the *u* [of *go*]. [The rule] *ā ṇi* [applies].

The suffix *ṇi* optionally occurs after words ending in short *a*, frequently; for example, from *dakkha*, the suffix *apacca* is added as *dakkhi*, thus forming *vāruṇi*. This rule applies frequently, but not to all words ending in *a*; thus, from *vasiṭṭha*, the form is simply *vāsiṭṭha* (the descendant of Vasiṣṭha).

From the word *rāja* (king), when another [patronymic] is intended within the sense of lineage (*jāti*), the suffix *ña* is added after the word *rāja*; thus, "the descendant of a king" is *rājañña*. Why "in the sense of lineage"? [To show: the mere descendant of a king [is] *rājāpacca*.

The suffix *yīya* [is applied] after the word *khatta*. After the word *khatta*, the suffixes *yeya* and *honta* occur in the sense of lineage (*jāti*). [Thus: from *khatta*, with the suffix *apacca*, we have *khattya* and *khattiya*; in the sense of lineage alone, *khatti*.
From *manu*, the suffixes *ssa* and *saṇa* [are applied].
From the word *manu*, the suffix *ssaṇ* occurs in the sense of lineage (*jāti*); thus, the descendant of Manu is a *manusso* (human), or a *mānuso*; likewise, one born in that lineage is a *mānavo*.
From the name of a country, the suffix *ṇo* occurs in the sense of a kṣatriya descendant and a king;
whatever is the name of a country, from that name, the suffix *ṇo* occurs in the sense of a kṣatriya descendant and a king—for example, the descendant of the Pañcālas is [Pāñcāla].

Is it "the king of Pañcāla" or "of the Magadha country"? What about "Dāsarathi" or "Khantiya"? [The suffix] *añ* is used for the descendant of a Brāhmaṇa from Pañcāla: *pañcālissa apaccaṃ* = *pañcāli*. With *kuru* and *sivi*, the suffix *ṇya* is used;
for the descendant or the king of the Kurus and Sivi, *ṇya* occurs: the descendant or king of the Kurus is *korabyo*. The suffix *sebbho* [is also used].
It is not "colored" by passion (*rāga*).

That by which one is colored is "passion"; thus, from the third-conjugation verbal root *raj* meaning "to color," the suffix *ṇa* occurs in the sense of "colored" (*ratta*)—as in "dyed with astringent juice" (*kasāvena rattaṃ kāsāvaṃ*), or "flower-colored" (*kosumhaṃ*).
Why is it not [used] here for "blue" or "yellow"? Because they are words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*), even without [the suffix].
Because it denotes that which does not exist [by itself].
The suffix *ṇa* occurs after a lunar mansion (*nakkhatta*) when it denotes time characterized by that mansion, provided that the mansion is conjoined with the moon; for example, *phusseṇa*.

The full moon day marked by the conjunction with the moon (*indu*) in the constellation Puṣya is *Phussī*; the full moon day marked by the conjunction with the moon in the constellation Maghā is *Māghī*.
[In the case of] "Māgho," the deity of that [constellation] is the full moon day.
[The suffix] *ṇa* occurs in the sense of the genitive after a word ending in the nominative; that which ends in the nominative and has two deities as its full moon day [takes this suffix].
*Sugata* means "one who has gone well"; *Sogata* refers to Māhinda. *Phussa* is so called because it is related to the full moon (*puṇṇamāsī*) of the month Phussa; likewise for Māgha.
One who has studied grammar knows [the rules] regarding the inclusion of words such as *vā*.
One who studies that and knows that is a *kaṇika*.
From the second [word] onwards, because of the rule "in these cases, *ṇa* occurs," there is *koṇika*.

And for the *veyyākaraṇa*, because of the substitution of *ya* for *ta*, according to the principle "those things which are like that become that," by the elision of vowels and so forth, and by the addition of *ekāra*, there are the forms *yāgama*, *dvittāni*, *ke*, *kamaka*, *padaka*, *ṇika*, and *suttantika*.

The suffix *ṇya* occurs after a word ending in the third case in the sense of "produced by that": from *kusamba*, "produced by *kusamba*," we have *kosambī* (the city). The suffix *ṇa* occurs after a word ending in the seventh case in the sense of "being there":

from *udaka*, "being in water," we have *odaka*. The suffix *tana* occurs after words beginning with *ajja* in the sense of "being": from *ajja*, "being today," we have *ajjatana*. Similarly, *hiyyo-tana* ("being yesterday"). By the rule "the letter *a* [is inserted] after *ña, ŋa, na, ma, va, ṇa" (*ñonamavaṇṇe*), the letter *a* is inserted; then, by the rule "after *sa* and *rambhā*, [the preceding vowel] becomes double" (*sarambhā dve*), the vowel *a* is doubled.

After *purāto* and *purā*, the suffix *ṇe* occurs in the sense of "being"; [with the addition of] *tana* and *va*, *purābhava* becomes *purāṇe* and *purātano*. [The suffix] *amā* is added after *tvaca*.

The suffix *am* occurs after *amā* in the sense of "being" (*bhava*); thus, from *amā-bhava*, we have *amacca*. From *majjha* and other [words] ending in the locative case, the suffix *ima* occurs in the sense of "being";
for example, in the analytical construction (*viggahe*) such as "being in the middle" (*majjhe bhavo*), we have *majjhima*, and "being at the end" (*ante bhavo*), we have *antima*, and so forth.
*Kaṇṇeyya*, *ṇeyyaka*, and *kayya*:

these suffixes ending in the locative case (*sattamyanta*) are used extensively in the sense of "being" (*bhavattha*). [Examples: *kaṇa*, *kosiṇaraka*, *ṇeyya*, *gaṅgeyyo*; *vāneyyo*, *ṇeyyaka*, *koleyyako*, *ya*, *gammo*;
elision of the short vowel *a*, prior forms; *iya*, *gamiyo*; *udariyaṃ*. The suffix *ṇika* occurs after words ending in the locative case in the sense of "being," as in *sarade bhāvo*.
The *sāradika* (autumnal) and the *hemantika* (winter).

The suffix *-ika* occurs in the sense of the genitive (*chaṭṭhatthe*) after words denoting "craft" (*sippa*), "virtue" (*sīla*), "merit" (*puñña*), "weapon" (*paharaṇa*), and "purpose" (*payojana*). For example, when "playing the lute" (*vīṇāvādana*) is his craft, he is called a *veṇika*.
One who possesses a bundle of grass is a *paṃjāsukūlika*; one whose trade is perfume is a *gandhika*; one whose weapon is a plow is a *vāpika*;
that which is worth a hundred is a *sātaka*. In all such cases, the suffix *-ika* occurs after a word ending in the second case, as in:
“He deserves to go, he wanders for alms”—thus *bhantā* [becomes] *bhantika*; *pakkhī* [becomes] *pakkhika*; *sākuṇī* [becomes] *sākuṇika*; and “it is worth a hundred” [becomes] *satika*.
One who goes to another’s wife is a *pāradārika*; one who gleans at *badara* trees is a *bādarika*; one who practices the Dhamma is a *dhammika*;

[and] an *adhammika*. [The suffix -ika is added] after a word ending in the third case (instrumental) when it has the sense of "done by that," "bought with that," "bound with that," "striven for by that," "mixed with that," "killed by that," "kills by that," "conquered by that," "conquers by that," "shines by that," "digs by that," "crosses by that," "wanders by that," "carries by that," or "lives by that."
It is *ṇika* because it is made by the body; *kāyika* because it is performed by the body; *sātika* because it was bought for a hundred;

*rattika* because it is bound with a leather strap; *ghatika* because it is prepared with ghee; *kasaṃsaṭṭha* because it is mixed with flour (meaning prepared through processing and mixed with flour);
*cālika* because it is struck with a net; *akkhika* because it is won with dice (meaning one wins or plays with dice).

Or, one who digs with a pickaxe is called a *khānittika*; here, the term *aṅgulikhantī* (“digging with a finger”) does not occur because it is not so designated, for the suffixes such as *ṇa* and compounds have that as their defining characteristic.
One who crosses by raft is a *oḷumpika*; one who travels by cart is a *sākaṭika*; one who carries on the shoulder is a *khandhika*;
one who lives by wages is a *vetanika*. [The suffix occurs] in the sense of “that leads to” (*tassa saṃvattati*).

The suffix *ika* occurs after words ending in the fourth case in the sense of "proceeding from" (*saṃvattati*), as in “*ponobhaviko*” (leading to renewed existence) and “*anādiyādīnamo maye ce*” (the homage beginning with ‘without beginning’).

It occurs after words ending in the fifth case in the sense of “originated from” (*tato sambhūtam āgataṃ*), such as *mātito sambhūtam āgataṃ* (originated from the mother), which is *māttikaṃ* (maternal), or *pettikaṃ* (paternal).
In the *Niggaṇṭhapada*, it is said: "Surabhito samabhūta.
Other conditions (*paccaya*) are also seen.

Other conditions besides those stated are seen in the sense of what has been stated and what has not been stated, such as *itiṇyo*, *sorabbhaṃ*. In that regard, there is the verse known by poets: "He dwells there... [and so forth].
"Appointed. One who dwells at the foot of a tree is a *rukkhamūlika*. Known in the world is *lokika*.

Those whose food is among the Four Great Kings are the *cātumahārājikā*. One appointed at the gate is a *dovārika* (gatekeeper). These are examples of such readings as "tadaminādi. This is its [meaning].

The suffix *ṇika* occurs after a word ending in the sixth case in the sense of "this belongs to. For example: *saṅghassa idaṃ* becomes *saṅghikaṃ*; *puggalikam*—here, by the suffix *ṇe*, it means "this belongs to Moggallāyana," as in *moggallāyanaṃ*.
(In grammar: *sogataṃ* (the teaching of the Buddha); (*the dispensation*). After the word *pitṛ* (father), the suffix *reyyaṇa* is used in the sense of a brother [of one's father].
The word *pitu* becomes *peyya* when followed by the suffix *-ya*. When followed by a suffix marked with *ra*, there is elision (*lopa*) of that component which has a vowel as its initial sound.

Since the vowel is at the beginning of that constituent part, there is elision of *u* according to the rule "when followed by a suffix marked with *ra*" (*rānubandhe*). Thus: *pitu* + *bhātā* = *petteyyo*.
And from the mother’s side, there is the sister (*bhaginī*).

From both the mother’s and the father’s side, there is their sister; that is, the mother’s sister (*mātubhaginī*) or maternal aunt (*mātucchā*)—having understood [the term] as “female” (*itthiyamattā*)—in this same way, there is the paternal aunt (*pitucchā*). [There is also] the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) and the paternal grandfather (*pitāmaha*).

Regarding mother and father: their mother’s mother is the maternal grandmother (*mātāmahī*); their mother’s father is the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaho*); their father’s mother is the paternal grandmother (*pitāmahī*); and their father’s father is the paternal grandfather (*pitāmaho*).
Regarding what is beneficial to mother and father: it is beneficial to mother and father when one is filial toward one’s mother (*matteyyo*) and filial toward one’s father (*petteyyo*).

The suffix *ṇika* is added after a word ending in the nominative case (*paṭhamantā*) in the sense of "this is its measure" (*parimāṇaṃ assa*), provided that the nominative-ending word is indeed a measure. For example:
*doṇo parimāṇam assa* becomes *doṇiko* ("measured by a *doṇa*"); likewise, *eko parimāṇam assa* becomes *ekako*, *dvikaṃ*, *tikaṃ*, *catukkaṃ*, *pañcakaṃ*, and so forth.
“Sañjātā” [is formed] by the rule beginning with “tārakādi.
From words beginning with “tāraka” ending in the nominative case, the suffix *ito* occurs in the sense of the genitive (*chaṭṭhī*).
Thus, when they have arisen—such as “tārakitaṃ” (the sky) having stars arisen, or “puṣpitaṃ” (a tree) having flowers arisen.

In the sense of "measure" (*māna*), the suffix *-mat* occurs after a word ending in the first case (*nominative*). For example: *phalakhalaṃ assa ummānaṃ* means "its measure is a basket," thus *phalakhalamattaṃ*; *hattho parimāṇam assa* means "its measure is a cubit," thus *hatthamattaṃ*; *sataṃ mānam assa* means "its measure is a hundred," thus *satamattaṃ*. And [the suffix] *ṇa* [occurs] after words meaning "man" (*purisa*).

The suffix *ṇa* occurs in the sense of "equal to" (*asseti*) after the word *purisa*, when it follows the first vowel (*paṭhamanta*) and ends in the masculine gender (*uddhamānavuttito*). Examples: *purisamattaṃ* (equal to a man), *purisatagghaṃ* (worth a man).
The suffixes *tta*, *tā*, *ttana*, *ṇya*, *ṇeyya*, *ṇigha*, and *ṇiyā* occur in the senses of abstract state (*bhāva*) and action (*kamma*).

That from which words and cognitions arise is the abstract state (*bhāva*); the cause for the occurrence of a word is the action (*kamma*), which is synonymous with activity (*kriyā*), moment (*chaṭā*), and so forth.
In the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*) and in the sense of object (*kamma*), suffixes such as *-tta* and *-tā* occur frequently; these are general rules that follow the usage [of the masters].
Sometimes they occur in both [senses], sometimes only in the sense of abstract state. However, they do not occur from every [base] in every [sense], except for *-tta* and *-tā*.

For example: *nīlassa paṭassa bhāvo* = *nīlattam*, *nīlatā*. Here, the abstract state is in the sense of a quality (*guṇa*). In this context, by virtue of the quality, the word *nīla* refers to the substance (*dabba*) endowed with the quality of blueness.
And cognition follows both the sign (nimitta) and the form (saru); thus it should be understood in other cases as well, according to what is appropriate.
For example: "the state of the quality blue" is blueness (*nīlattam*), or "blueness" (*nīlatā*); "the genus and lineage of the quality blue" is "cowness" (*gotā*), or "cowness" (*gojāti*);

"the state of being a cooker" is the connection with the act of cooking; "the king’s man" is the connection with the king; "Devadatta’s moonness" or "sunness" is the commonality of those particular states; and "space-ness" (*ākāsattam*) [is the same].
*Abhāvat-tan*: the commonality of the metaphorical distinction; *alasassa bhāvo* or *kammaṃ* = *alasattaṃ*, *alasatā*;
*-ttaṇa* = *puthujjanattaṇaṃ*; *-ṇya* = *cāpakalyaṃ*; *sakattheti* = *sakatthe pi akiñcanam eva* = *ākiñcaññaṃ*;
*-ṇeya* = *soceyyaṃ*; *-avaṅa-iya* = *pāṭavaṃ*; *-ṇiya* = *naggiyaṃ*; *-ya* = *porohitiyaṃ*.
*Tara* [is used] after *tamissī*.
Because they occur after a word expressing excellence (*atisaya*), these are suffixes of excellence: *pāpataro*, *pāpatamo*, *pāpissiko*, *pāpiyo*, *pāpiṭṭho*.
Even from a word already expressing excellence, there is a suffix of further excellence: *pāpiṭṭhataro*. [As in: *udumbarassa*...
In the analysis [of compounds] such as *vikāra* (modification) and *avayava* (part), the suffixes *ṇa*, *ṇika*, and *ṇeya* are not applied.

A modification (*vikāra*) is a subsequent state different from the original material (*pakati*); therefore, after a noun ending in the sixth case, the suffixes *ṇa* and others are applied to denote a modification or a part.
In the case of compounds such as *bahulaṃ-ṇa*, *odumbaraṃ-ṇika*, *kappāsikaṃ-neyya*, and *eṇeyyaṃ-maya*, the suffixes *ṇa*, *ṇika*, *neyya*, and *maya* are applied.

Similarly, in the case of *tiṇamayaṃ* ("made of grass"), even when there is a shift in meaning (*atthantare*), the term *gomayaṃ* ("cow-dung") refers to the manure of cattle. In the case of the compound *manussānaṃ samūho* ("an assembly of people"), and so forth, these are examples of such grammatical formations (*viggahe*).

The suffix *kaṇṇa* occurs after words ending in the sixth case (*chaṭṭhī*) to denote a collection (*samūha*). Examples: *mānussakaṃ*, *kākaṃ*, *āpūpikaṃ*. Regarding the rule “after *jana* and so forth, *tā*”: the suffix *tā* occurs after these to denote a collection. Examples: *janatā* (a collection of people), *gajatā* (a collection of elephants), *bandhutā* (a collection of kinsmen).
The suffix *kā* occurs when there is only one crow (*ekā kākyasahāye*).
From *eka* in the sense of "alone," *ka* and *ki* are the suffixes:
*ekova ekako*, *ekākī*.
From *ubho-dvitīhaṃsa*, with the first-case endings of the two parts (*upadvitīhi avayavavuttīhi*), the suffix *aya* occurs in the sense of the genitive: *ubho aṃsā assa*.
Both. Two. Three. In the section on ordinal numbers (*pūraṇa-saṅkhyā*) beginning with "one" (*eka*), by the rule of grammatical derivation (*nipātana*):

“The fourth and second [are formed] from these; the third and first [from those],” the suffix *iya* is applied in the sense of an ordinal. From *dvi*, *tiya* is substituted, and for *dvi*, *du* is also substituted. From *tri* and *catu*, the suffix *tha* is added. Thus: *dvitīya*, *tṛtīya*, *caturtha*. [The suffix *ma* is applied] after *pañca* and so forth, according to how many [there are].

The suffix *mo* is substituted for the final vowel of numerals beginning with five (*pañca*) and ending with six (*chaṭṭhi*), in the sense of completion. For example: *pañcamo* (the fifth), meaning the completion of five; likewise, *sattamo*, *aṭṭhamo*, and so forth.
[In the case of six: *chaṭṭha* and *ṭṭhama*. From the word *cha*, the forms *ṭṭha* and *ṭṭhama* arise in the sense of completion—the completion of six is *chaṭṭho* or *chaṭṭhamo*.

After a numeral beginning with *ekādasa* (eleven) and ending in the sixth case (*chaṭṭhivibhatti*), the suffix *ḍa* is optionally applied in the sense of "completing" (*pūraṇa*). The letter *ḍa* is an *anubandha*. When completing the number eleven, it becomes *ekādaso*; otherwise, it is *ekādasama*. Likewise, *dvādaso*, and so forth. After numbers beginning with *ekūnavīsati* (nineteen), the suffix *tuṭ* is applied. [The *ṭ* is an *anubandha*] for the sake of the *sa* sound; [the result is] *tissa*.
It appears that there is the elision (*lopa*) of the suffix *tikā* when it follows *sant*. This is called *tilopa*. [The number] nineteen. And for numbers beginning with *sata*:

after a numeral beginning with *sata* ending in the genitive case, the suffix *mo* is substituted in the sense of "completing" (*pūraṇa*), and for the words *sata* and so on, there is the substitution of the final vowel *a*.
