The suffix *ghyaṇ* occurs after roots ending in the vowel *ā*, in the senses of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). The substitution of *e* for *ā* is prescribed by the rule “*āssa e ca-dānaṃ dīyatīti vā deyyaṃ*. In the sense of the abstract state and the object, according to the rule “*vada-pacane vadādīhi yo*,” the suffix *ya* is applied to roots beginning with *vada*.

In the case of roots where the preceding group of consonants is *ca-vagga* (palatals), there is the substitution of the preceding form (*pubbarūpa*). Thus: *vadanaṃ* (the act of speaking) or *vaditabbaṃ* (that which is to be spoken) = *vajjaṃ*. For the root *gama* (to go), because it belongs to the class beginning with *vada*, the suffix *ya* is applied: *gamanaṃ* (the act of going) or *gamyate* (it is gone to) = *gamyaṃ*.
For the root *guha* (to conceal), according to the rule “*guhādīhi yaka*,” the suffix *yaka* is applied in the senses of the abstract state and the object.
The letter *ka* in *yaka* serves the purpose of making [the preceding vowel] a nasalized suffix (*kānubandha*).

When a light (*lahu*) semi-vowel (*yuvaṇṇa*) that has a light penultimate (*upanta*) follows, the letters *e* and *o* respectively become the suffixes, according to the rule "when a suffix (*paccaya*) occurs. This refers to the attainment of the letter *so*.

In the phrase “*na te kānubandhanāgamesu*,” there is the inclusion of a prohibition (*paṭisedha*). *Guhaṇaṃ* means that which is to be hidden; *kavā* refers to the secret (*guyha*); this is a permutation (*vipallāsa*). In the sense of instruction (*sāsa*) and exhortation (*anusaṭṭhi*), the suffix *-ya* is applied.

Or, it is the head (*sisa*) of the instruction (*sāsa*). Or, the head of the instruction becomes [the suffix] when followed by a *kā*-consonant suffix; after the application of the initial form (*pubbarūpa*), one who is instructed is called a *sisso*. In the alternative where the substitution of *siso* does not occur—

[The suffix] *ñi* [is applied] after a verbal root (*byañjana*) that has an action as its meaning (*kriyattha*), when followed by another suffix beginning with *byañjana*, such as *paccaya*. The letter *ñ* in *ñi* is for the purpose of specification, according to the rule "after *ñi* [comes] *lassa*" (*ñilasse*). Alternatively, because the governing rule (*adhikāra*) is established as an option (*vavatthitavibhāsattā*), the absence of *ñi* should be understood in some instances. [The suffixes] *la*, *tu*, and *ṇaka* are used in the sense of the agent (*kattari*).

In the sense of a *kāraka* (participant in an action), verbal roots meaning "action" (*kriyāttha*) take the suffixes *la*, *tu*, and *na*. The letter *l* in the rule “*latupitādanamā simhī*” is for the purpose of specification. One who gives is a *dātā* (giver); with the suffix *ṇaka*, there is the augment *yuk*.

For a verbal root ending in *a* that means "action," the augment *yuk* occurs before the suffix *ṇa* when followed by another suffix having *ṇ* as its *anubandha*; thus, *dāyaka*. For the root *vadh* (to kill/injure)—by the rule “*ñibyañjanassā”*—the *ñi* [is elided]; one who kills is a *vadhitā*. With the suffix *ṇaka*, by the rule “*assānanubandhe*,” when the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel (*assa*) has occurred, [the form becomes *vadhaka*].
Also elsewhere.

Regarding the prohibition that "e, o, and ā do not sometimes occur [as substitutes] for the suffix -anū" even in cases other than those derived from *kānubandha* (suffixes with the marker *n*): [this applies] in *paṭāsedho*, *vadhako*, and *lucchedane*. [And] where does *vaṇa* occur?
After a verbal root (*kamma*), the suffix *aṇ* occurs in some instances when the sense is that of an action (*kriyāttha*) and the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed;

[the resulting suffixes] are *āya*, *āva*, or *ā*, provided they have *ṇ* as their indicatory letter (*ṇ-anubandha*). When *ṇ* is the indicatory letter, *ñ*, *ṇ*, *m*, *āy*, and *āva* occur respectively after vowels; there is substitution (*vādesa*) for the vowel [of the root]. Thus, "one who cuts grass" is *saralāva*.
"One who makes a pot is a *kumbhakāra*. Why [is it] "somewhere"? [Because of the example: *kammakāra*. Here, the suffix *ghaṇ* or *gha* occurs by the rule:

"In the case of the agent of the action (*bhāvakāraka*), there are *ghaṇ* and *gha*. This is seen in the context of looking at the direction. The directions [are formed] from a common base, another base, the word *bhavanta*, and so on, when used as a comparison; [the suffixes] *rī* and *ikkhaka* are applied after words such as *samāna* and others, and after comparisons expressed by words beginning with *yā*.
In the case of *kammakārake*, they become *rīrikkhakā*. According to the rule “*rānubandhe'ntasarādissā*,” when the *is*-portion of the suffix (*dis*) is elided,
and there is the substitution of *sā* for *samāna*— as in *sadī* (meaning "one who will show like a similar one") and *sadikkho*— these do not undergo the elision of the *kānubandha*.
In the absence of *te*, *e*, *o*, *ā*, *kānubandha*, and *nāgama*, [the suffix] *sadisa* occurs.

Regarding *samāna*: "After the word *samāna*, the substitute *ra* optionally occurs for the following sound *sa*, except when *rī* or *rikka* follow. Thus, by the substitution of *ra* for *da* in the alternative case: *sarī*, *sarikkho*, *sariso*.
The suffix *ā* is substituted for the words beginning with *sabba* when followed by *añña*, *ādika*, or *ādissa*. [Examples: *aññādī*, *aññādiko*, *aññādiso*.
For the words ending in *nta*, *kim*, and *ima*, the suffixes *ṭā*, *kī*, and *ṭī* are applied respectively.
Now, what are these *ṭā*, *kī*, and *ṭī* for the sounds in the nominative cases? They are, respectively, *ṭa*-forms used for the purpose of universal substitution (*sabbādesattha*):
*bhavādī*, *bhavādikkho*, *bhavādiso*; *yādi*, *yādikkho*, *yādiso*; *tyādikkho*, *tyādiso*, and so forth; and *tumhāmhā*, *tā*. This is the distinction.
For the [pronoun] *tumhāmhānaṃ*, there is only *tā* in the singular.

In the sense of "like us" (*tādi*), "like me" (*mādi*), "of such a kind" (*tādikkho*), "of such a kind" (*mādikkho*), "such as that" (*tādiso*), and "such as me" (*mādiso*), [the suffix -ika is applied]. In the sense of "one like you" (*tumhādiso*) and "one like us" (*amhādiso*), [the suffix -ika is applied] when there is a collection [of persons].
In the sense of state (*bhāva*) and agent (*kāraka*), the suffixes *a*, *ghaṇ*, *gha*, and *ka* occur frequently after verbal roots; [specifically,] *a* occurs after the root *iss*.
*Ñonamayavā sare*:

when *sare* follows, the *ñonamayava* sounds occur according to their respective order, and there is the substitution of *ay*. *Ciya-ti vācayo-nīpāpuṇane*: "to reach" (*nīpāpuṇane*) is from the root *vāc* with the suffix *-yo*. *Vinaya-naṃ*: "discipline" (*vinaya*) is from the prefix *vi-* plus *nī* in the sense of leading away (*pubbovinayanaṃ*), or from *vi-* plus *neti* ("to lead"), hence "discipline.

*Rava-naṃ ravo*: "sound" (*ravo*) is from the root *ru* in the sense of making sound (*sadde*). *Bhavanaṃ bhavo*: "existence" (*bhavo*) is from the root *bhu* in the sense of being (*sattāyaṃ*). *Gaha*: [the root] *gah* (to grasp).

In the case of *upādāna* (clinging), [the root] *pra* is prefixed; *paggaṇhaṇaṃ* means grasping (*paggaho*). The roots *gada*, *dapa*, *raṇa*, *sara*, *vara*, *cara*, etc., and the roots *gaha*, etc., have the sense of seizing (*gaha*).

With respect to the sense of "doing" (*karaṇe*), when the suffix *du* expresses difficulty (*kicchatthe*) and not ease, it is called *dukkara* because it is done with difficulty (*dukkhena karīyati*);

or when it expresses ease (*akicchatthesu*), such as in the prefixes *īsaṃ*, *susu*, *cu*, *ppa*, it is called *īsakkara* because it is done easily (*sukhena karīyati*), or *sukkara*. And *caja* has the sense of abandoning (*hāniyaṃ*); *ghaṇa* is the act of abandoning (*cajanaṃ*).

*Pāka* (cooking) is preceded by *pubba*. *Nipaka* means "one who cooks" (*pacati*), derived from *ni* + *paca* + *ka*. *Khipaka* means "one who throws," derived from *khipa* (to throw) + *ka*. *Pītappaṇe*: [The suffix] *iya* and *uṇa* are added after verbal roots ending in *ivaṇṇa* and *uvaṇṇa* before a vowel.

According to the rule "the suffixes *iya* and *uṇa* are added to verbal roots ending in *ivaṇṇa* and *uvaṇṇa* before a vowel in certain instances," *iyaṅ* is applied. *Piyo* is derived from *ṇī* (to lead) + *ya*. *Abhibhu* is derived from *bhu* (to exist) with *abhi* preceding it.
The suffix *kvi* frequently becomes *kya* in the meanings of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the agent (*kāraka*). [The suffix] *issa* occurs after it.

In the case of a verbal root (*kriyāttha*), when the suffix *kv* is elided after another [suffix], there is the elision of *kv*. Thus: from *abhibhavati*, by the elision of *kv*, it becomes *abhibhū*;

likewise, *sayambhū*. From the root *gam* (to go), with the suffix *kv*: “when *kv* follows, there is elision of the final consonant,” thus the *m* is elided, resulting in *urago* (from *urasā gacchati*).

From the root *dā* (to give): “after *an*,” in the sense of the agent of the action (*bhāvakāraka*), the suffix *ana* is added; *dā + ana* becomes *dānaṃ* (that which is given). From the prefix *saṃ* and the preceding [root]: *sammā*.

That from which something is given is the *sampadāna* (recipient); that from which [something] is taken away is the *apādāna* (ablative), as in "he takes away from this"; the *karaṇa* (instrument) is used in the sense of doing;

that which is placed above is the *adhi* (locative prefix)—by the rule "rā nassa ṇe," it becomes *ṇe*; that in which something is located is the *adhikaraṇa* (locative); *gaha* is used in the sense of grasping. Likewise, for *tatha*, there are *ṭa, ṭha, ṇa, la*.

For *ta*, *tha*, *na*, and *ra*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ṇa*, and *la* may occur respectively; [the substitution] should be understood as applying to the place of *ṇa*. The prefix *ni-* occurs before the root *gam-*. In certain instances, *yu* occurs after words such as *pada*.

In certain suffixes, *yu* occurs after words such as *pada*; [the forms] *nipatti* (attainment) and *nipajjana* (lying down) also occur. In *tappaṇa* (causing to heat), when followed by the suffix *ana*, there is the substitution of *n* for *v* and so forth.
And by the words "ca'na te" and so forth, [it is shown that] there is no [elision of] "e". "Pī" means nourishment; "ji" is used in the senses of fear and movement;

"saṃ" is a prefix meaning agitation—"saṃvijanaṃ" means causing agitation. "Aññatrāpi" means even in the absence of these [prefixes]. "Saṃvijanaṃ" means being agitated. "Kudha" is used in the sense of anger—one who is angry by nature is "kodhana. "Bhikkha" is used in the sense of begging.
In the feminine gender, the suffixes "ṇa," "kti," "ka," "yaka," and "yā" are used.

In the sense of femininity, state, and agent, the suffixes *ā* and others occur after verbal roots, as well as *ana* frequently. Regarding *bhikkhā*: from the root *bhikkh*, the suffix *ā* is applied; alternatively, the suffix *āpaccaya* is applied, and the letter *ṇ* causes the substitution of *kāra*. Thus, *kārā* means a prison.
The formation of words occurs in whatever manner is appropriate through conventional usage, and the determination of meaning is based on established tradition.

From the root *bhid*, meaning "to split," the suffix *kti* is applied, resulting in *bhedana* (splitting). Alternatively, *bhitti* is formed from the root *bhid* with the suffix *i*; or from the root *ruj*, meaning "to break," with the suffix *ka*: that which breaks is *ruja*. Thus, *rujati* means "it breaks."
*Vijjā*: "They know through this" (*etāya vidanti*), thus it is *vijjā*. Alternatively, from the root *vaj* meaning "to go," with the prefix *vi-* and the suffix *-ja*, it is *pabbajjā*.

According to the rule of grammatical analysis (*yogavibhāga*) stating "the substitution of *ca* for *va*," the *v* becomes *b*, hence *pabbajjā*. *Vandanā*: from the roots *vand* and *añc* used in the senses of salutation and praise; the suffix *-ana* forms *vandana*, which is *vandanā*. [The following applies] when the preceding and succeeding sounds are identical (*sarūpe*).

When a verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in *i* follows another verbal root that expresses its own form, the suffixes *ki*, *tī*, and *i* are applied—this is according to the rule "the verbal root itself [is used] when followed by *vaci*, *kimhi*, *yudhi*, and *ti* in the *tim* [case].
Because the suffix *lo* is known from the rule "for the agent, *lo*" (*kattari lo*), there arise forms such as *pacati* (from *pac-*) and *katheti* (from *katha-*).

[The word] *kāra* [in the commentary] is a genitive compound with the word ending in the suffix *ghaṇ*: "its *kāra*," meaning its vowel (*akāra*). [The root] *bhuja* is used in the senses of protecting and eating.

The suffix *ṇī* occurs after the words *sīla*, *abhikkhañña*, and *avassaka* when they are understood as having the sense of an action (*kriyattha*). For example: from *sīla* comes *uṇhabhojī* (one who eats hot food) in the sense of “he eats hot [food] by habit”;

from *pāna* (drinking), according to the rule “*yuka* follows *assāṇa* and *pimha*,” comes *khīrapāyī* (one who drinks milk) in the sense of “he drinks even milk”; from *avassaṃ* (necessarily), *avassakārī* (one who acts necessarily); and from *satam avassaṃ dadāti* (he gives a hundred necessarily), *satandāyī* (one who gives a hundred).
The suffixes *ktavantu* and *ktāvi* are used for the past tense (*bhūte*) when the action is completed (*parisamatte*) or attained (*atte*).

From a present tense verbal root (*vattamānato*), these suffixes—*kta*, *anta*, *tu*, and *ktāvi*—are added to express the agent (*kattari*). For example: from *abhuñji* (he ate), we have *bhuttavā* (one who has eaten); from *asuṇi* (he heard), we have *sutavā* or *sutāvī* (one who has heard). The suffix *kta* is also used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the passive/objective (*kamme*).

The suffix *kta* occurs after verbal roots (*bhū*) in the sense of the action itself (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). [Examples: *āsa* in the sense of sitting (*upavesana*): *āsanaṃ āsitaṃ*; *ñi-ru* in the sense of weeping (*rodana*): *vā kvaci*.

In some instances, the letters *e*, *o*, and *ā* do not occur when there is the elision of the suffix *kānu*. [Examples: *rodanaṃ ruditaṃ*; "it was made to weep" (*roditaṃ karīyittha*) is thus called *kata*.
There is elision of the final [consonant] of *gam* and so forth.

There is elision of the final [consonant] of words beginning with *gam* and ending in *r*, when a suffix beginning with *t* and having *k* as its *anubandha* follows, provided it is not one that causes the doubling of the preceding consonant (*katvāvajjita*). [Example: *yāpāpuṇane*.

The suffix *kta* occurs after roots meaning "going" (*gamanattha*), after intransitive roots (*akammaka*), and after roots meaning "action" (*kriyattha*) when used in the sense of a locus (*ādhāra*), as well as in the senses of the agent (*kartṛ*) and the passive/objective state (*bhāva-kamma*). Examples: *Yātavantaṃ asmiṃ ti yātaṃ* (a place where one has gone).

*Yātavantā yānā* (those who have gone by means of vehicles). *Yānaṃ yātaṃ* (the vehicle that has been traveled). *Yāyitthāti yāto* (the path that has been traversed). *Āsitavanto asmiṃ ti* (that in which those who have sat exist).
*Āsitaṃ* (the place), *āsitavanto*, *āsitā*, *āsanaṃ*, *āsitaṃ*—these are the forms.

*Netā*: when the agent (*kattari*) is expressed in the present tense (*vattamāne*), the suffix *nto* occurs after a verbal root (*kriyatthā*) that expresses an action which has begun but is not yet completed.
The suffix *lo* [is used].

From the sense of *kuyattha* (the agent), *lo* occurs in place of the *l*-suffixes such as *āna*, which are prescribed for the agent (*kattṛ*) when they are proximate; the letter *l* is for the purpose of specification [by the rule] “*ñi lasse*” (Pāṇini 7.1.3). Thus, *pavati* becomes *pavanto*; *māno* is the agentive form (*kattari māno*), as in *pacamāno*. [This applies] to the states of being (*bhāva*) and the objects (*karman*).
The suffix *māna* occurs after verbal roots (*kriyāttha*) in the sense of the present tense, expressing both the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*).

The suffix *kyo* occurs after other suffixes such as *mānantā* and so forth—specifically those prescribed for the abstract action and the object (*bhāvakamma*), excluding the remote past (*parokkhā*)—where the letter *ka* is used to indicate the absence of vowel strengthening (*avuddhi*). Thus: in the sense of the abstract action, from the root *bhū*, we have *bhuyamānaṃ*; in the sense of the object, from the root *pac*, we have *paccamāno*.

The suffixes *ssapubba*, *anāgata*, *anāraddha*, and *vattamānato* [are applied] to verbal roots (*kriyattha*) to form the future tense; they take the endings *-nta* and *-māna*. Within their respective domains, when the agent (*kattari*) is expressed by the suffix *-ñi*, we have:

*pacissati* (he will cook) → *pacissanto*; *pacissamāno* (he will be cooking). When the action itself (*bhāve*) is expressed: *bhavissati* (it will be) → *bhavissamānaṃ*. When the object (*kamme*) is expressed: *paccissati* (it will be cooked) → *paccissamāno*. When the instrument (*karaṇe*) is expressed: *karissati* (he will do) → *karissamāno*.
The suffixes *tuṃ*, *tāye*, and *tave* occur in the sense of the future tense (*bhavissati*) for the purpose of that action;

they are used in the sense of the future (*bhavissati-atthe*) after verbal roots (*kriyatthā*) when expressing the state (*bhāve*) and when the action is understood as being for the sake of that [other action].

Regarding the rule “*tuṃ-tuṇa-tabbesu vā*,” the vowel *a* [of the suffix] undergoes elision (*vā-akāro*), and otherwise, the single-substitute form (*pararūpaṃ*) applies. This occurs in the sense of the instrumental (*karaṇaya*).
He goes to do; he goes to do for the sake of doing—[in the phrase] “he will do” (*karassā tave*), [the suffix] *tave* is used in the sense of *ākātave*;
what does it signify? It signifies the action, as in “he goes thinking, ‘I shall do’. What does it signify? It signifies the purpose, as in “he has matted hair thinking, ‘I shall beg for alms’.
For one who is going, there will be food for you—for eating; [the suffix] *gaha* is used in the sense of grasping or taking.
Of those actions that have a single agent:

when there are actions having one agent, the suffixes *tu*, *na*, *ka*, and *tvā* are applied to the root signifying that which is prior among them; this is for the sake of the object (the action itself), and occurs in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*). Furthermore, the *e* of *etva* becomes *i*.

*Eilānaṃ* occurs: having performed the act of grasping (*gaṇhaṇaṃ*), one goes; having taken (*gahetūna*), one goes; having grasped (*gahetvā*). This is because [the suffix] *tvā* belongs to the *rudh*-class and others.

Or, for the *rudh*-class and others, there is optionally *maṃ*. According to the alternative where there is optionally *maṃ* as a suffix for the *rudh*-class and others, *maṃ* occurs. Furthermore, because it is followed by the letter *m*, the vowel *a* follows.

*Ṇe* replaces *niggahīta*. For the *niggahīta* of *gaha*, *ṇe* occurs: *gaṇhi tuna*, *gaṇhitvāna*, *gaṇhitvā*. Why [is it] "when there is a single agent"? Example: *devadatte bhuttasmiṃ yaññadatto gacchati*.
Why [is it] "after [the preceding action]"? Example: *bhuñjati ca pacati ca*. Why [is it] "not having reached"? Example: *appatvā*.
"A mountain becomes a river" after crossing a precipice: because the root *bhū* (to become) occurs in all cases, it is understood that there is a single agent and a prior temporal sequence.
Therein, the gender is shown entirely according to the predominant usage.
The specific details, however, are to be understood by the wise from the sequence of the recitation.

[Now follow] *tabbādayo* (the suffixes beginning with *-tavya*). Now the suffixes beginning with *tya* are being stated: when *paca* (to cook) stands as *paca*, the rule "kriyatthā bahulam" (the verbal roots are used diversely) applies everywhere.
In the present tense (*vattamāna*), the suffixes *anti*, *asi*, *tha*, *mhi*, *ante*, *se*, *vega*, and *emhe* are used.
When the sense commenced in the present is completed, the forms beginning with *kriy-attha* (the third person) and so forth are used for the present; their application is as follows:

for the six preceding and following persons, whether singular or plural, when referring to "you" (*tumha*) and "we" (*amha*), there are two sets each for the middle and highest persons, and the first person.

In the case of agents expressed by words denoting one, many, or plural, as well as those expressed by other words, the first, second, and third persons—both the preceding and the following sets of six—take two endings each, namely the middle and the highest, respectively, according to the sense of the action (*kriyāttha*). When expressing a single [agent], the singular number is used;
thus, *ti*, *ti*, and *anti* are designated as the first person because they are taught at the beginning, while *si* and *tha* are the middle person.

Having thus indicated "me" (*ma*) as the first person, this supreme term *uttama* (first person) expresses the two endings beginning with the third person (*tṛtīya*) and so forth by their inherent nature.

In this way, it should be applied respectively to the subsequent cases where the agent (*kartṛ*), object (*karman*), and state (*bhāva*) are prescribed; for instance, in rules such as "the suffixes *kyal* etc.
occur [in the sense of] state and object" (*kyo bhāvakammesu*) and "the suffix *lo* occurs for the agent in the first person" (*mānantatyādisu kattari lo*). Thus it is to be understood.

Since the suffixes beginning with *tya* are understood to express the agent (*kattṛ*), the object (*karman*), and the state (*bhāva*), when the agent is expressed, the suffix *ti* is added; after this, *lo* [is applied], as in *pacati*. In the plural, when the agent is to be expressed, *anti* is added.

In some instances, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*). Since there is an elision of the verbal suffix in certain cases, the vowel *ā* of the suffix *lassa* is elided, resulting in *pavanti*, *pacasi*, and *pacatha*.

Before *himi* suffixes, the vowel *a* becomes long. [Examples: *pacāmi*, *pacāma*; in the second person plural (*pacatha*), *pacate*, *pacante*; *pacase*, *pacavhe*; *pace*, *pacāmhe*. In the passive voice (*kamme*), by the rule beginning with "accādi," the suffix *kyo* is applied for the states of being (*bhāva*) and the object (*kamma*).
[Example: *kyassa*.
In the case of a verbal root (*kriyāttha*) denoting an action performed for another, the suffix *īna* or the letter *ñ* occurs; here, the letter *ñ* signifies the initial portion [of the suffix].
Thus: *pacīyati*, *paccati*. Regarding the rule *gurupubbā rassāre’nte’ntīnaṃ*:
after a short vowel (*rassa*) preceded by a heavy syllable (*guru*), the letter *re* optionally replaces the suffixes *ante* and *anti*. Thus: *pacīyare*, *pacīyanti*; *paccare*, *paccanti*.
*pacīyasi*, *paccasi*, *pacīyatha*, *paccatha*; *pacīyāmi*, *paccāmi*, *pacīyāma*, *paccāma*—and in the passive (*bhāve*):
*pacīyate*, *paccate*, *pacīyare*, *pacīyante*, *paccare*, *paccante*; *pacīyase*, *paccase*, *pacīyavhe*, *paccavhe*; *pacīye*, *pacce*, *pacīyāmhe*, *paccāmhe*.
Since the state (*bhāva*) and existence (*sattā*) are singular, there is only the singular number; and that [is as follows].
[The suffix] occurs only in the first person: *devadattena sambhavati* or *bhuyati*, or *buyate devadattassa*; the meaning is "Devadatta is currently becoming.
This is because [the rule] *nehiña bahulaṃ* prescribes [the suffix] extensively.

Even those that are intransitive become transitive when used in the passive voice (*ṇiṇappanta*);
those that are transitive may have two objects, or they may have two objects [in the passive], or three objects.

Examples include: *bhavissati*, *pācayissati*, *pācessati*, *pācayissare*, *pācayissanti*, *pācessare*, *pācessanti*; and in the case of the object: *pācīyissati* (with elision of the *ya*-suffix), *pācissati*, etc.; and in the past tense: *apācayittha*.
He caused to cook: *apācayat*, *apācayattha*; he caused to cook: *pācayattha*, *apācettha*, *pācettha*; he caused to cook: *apācayi*, *pācayi*.
They caused to cook: *apācayī*, *pācayī*, *apācayisu*, *pācayisu*, *apācayamsu*, *pācayamsu*. They knew (*ñottā*). May they be well (*suṃ*).
From the substitution of *ñā* and *o*, for another person (*parassa*) in the future tense, there are:
*sum*, *apācayasuṃ*, *pācayasuṃ*, *apācesuṃ*, *pācesuṃ*, *apācayuṃ*, *pācayum*, and so forth; this is the specific rule for *ussa*. In the passive (*kamme*), there are:
*apācīyittho*, *pācīyittho*, *apācīyattho*, *pācīyattho*, *apāciyi*, *pācīyi*, *apāciyī*, *pācīyi*, and so forth; in the non-past tense (*anajjatane*), there are: *apācayattha*, *pācayattha*.
*Apācettha*, *kapācettha*, *apācaya*, *pācaya*, *apācayā*, *pācayā*, *apācayu*, *pācayu*, *apācayū*, *pācayū*—and so forth; likewise for the middle voice (*parokkha*):
*apācīyattha*, *pācīyattha*, *apācīya*, *pācīya*, *apācīyā*, *pācīyā*—and so forth. [In these cases,] there is shortening of the preceding vowel.
In the second person of the past tense, the vowel becomes short: *papācayi*, *papācayu*, *papācaye*, *papācayittha*, *papācettha*, and so forth.

In the passive (*kamma*), everything is the same as in the active (*kattū*); for example: *apācayi*, *pācayi*, *apācayissa*, *pācayissa*, *apācayissā*, *pācayissā*, *apācayissaṃsu*, *pācayissaṃsu*, and so forth. In the passive (*kamma*): *apāciyi*, *pāciyi*, *apācīyissa*, *pācīyissa*.

In the case of the causal suffix (*ṇi*), as in *pāceti*, *pācayati*, *pācayate*, *pācayati*, etc., for the roots *pac* and *pac* (to cook); in the case of the resultative suffixes (*hetuphala*), as in *pācaye*, *pācayeyya*, *pācayuṃ*, *pācayeyyum*, etc.;

in the case of the passive suffixes (*kamma*), as in *pācīye*, *pācīyeyyum*, etc.; in the case of the gerund suffixes (*tvādi*), as in *pācayatu*, *pācetū*, *pācayantu*, *pācentu*, etc.; in the case of the passive suffixes (*kamma*) again, as in *pācīyatu*, *pācīyantu*, etc.;

and in the case of the causative suffix (*ṇapi*), as in *pācāpayati*, *pācāpeti*, etc.—which are identical to those formed with the primary suffix (*nyanta*)—the suffix *ṇi* is also applied even after a form ending in *ṇi*. Thus it is said: "It is employed for the purpose of causing to cook. Even from a form ending in *ṇi*, the suffix *ṇi* occurs.
*Ṇiṇapinaṃ tesu*.

Regarding *ṇī* and *ṇapi*: there is elision (*lopo*) of *na* in those [suffixes] *ṇī* and *ṇapi*. Thus, after the elision of the preceding *ṇi*, one should understand it in all cases as *pācayati*, *pāceti*, and so forth—such is the rule for *ṇapi*.
This is the method for the *bhū*-class and others.

Now, for the purpose of explaining the classification of the *vikaraṇas*, some forms of each individual verbal root beginning with the first of the eight classes (*gaṇa*)—starting with *rudh* and so forth—are cited.
And among the roots beginning with *rudh*:

after a root such as *rudh*, when the suffixes *āna*, *tati*, and others are prescribed for a proximate agent (*aparokkhe sukattari*), the form *rundhati* occurs, where the vowel *o* at the end of the root *rudh* is replaced by *u*.

In the *rundhati*, *rundhanti*, etc., in the *rudh*-class (the seventh class), it should be understood everywhere that the suffix *-ma* is applied according to the rule “*maṃ vā rudhādīnaṃ*,” resulting in forms such as *ruṇṇhiyati* or *rujjhati*.
This is the method for the *rudh*-class.
The root *div* is used in the senses of playing, desiring victory, commerce, splendor, praise, and going.

The suffix *yaka* is added after roots beginning with *div* when the sense is that of the agent (*la*). The letter *k* is an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) for the purpose of causing the application of the suffix *kā*. Thus, in the subsequent examples: *dibbati*, *dibbare*, *dibbanti*, etc. In the passive sense (*kamme*): *diyīyati*, *dibbati*, *divīyare*, *diviyanti*, *dibbare*, *dibbanti*, etc.
This is the method for roots beginning with *div*.
*Tuda* means to afflict. After *tuda* and other such roots, the suffix *ka* occurs.

After *tuda* and other such roots, when *la* (the optative) is the object, *ka* occurs—as in *tudati*, *tudanti*, etc. In the passive (*kamma*), it becomes *tudyati*, *tujjati*, *tudyare*, *tudiyan*, *tujjare*, *tudyanti*, etc.
The rule for *tud* and so forth.
*Ji* [becomes] *jaye*. [The suffix] *ktā* [is applied] after *jyā* and others.
The *ji* group [of roots] occurs in the sense of sound (*kalaviṣaya*): *jināti*, *jinanti*, etc., and in the sense of action (*kamma*): *jiyati*, *jiyare*, *jiyanti*, etc.
This is the method for the *jyā* group. The root *kī* occurs in the sense of bending or curving (*dabbavinīmaya*).
By *ky-ādi* [suffixes], *kaṇ* is substituted. By *kī-ādi* [suffixes], *kaṇ* occurs when there is a vowel (*la*) in the domain.
In the case of knowledge (*nāṇa*), it is short.

In the case of a verbal root (*kriyattha*) ending in *n*, the short vowel occurs: *kiṇati* (he buys), *kiṇanti* (they buy), etc.; in the passive (*kamme*): *kīyati* (it is bought), *kīyare* (they are bought), *kīyanti* (they are bought), etc.
This is the method for roots beginning with *k*. [The suffix] *su* is used in the sense of hearing (*savaṇe*).
*Svādīhi keṇā*:

By means of the *ke* suffix, [the verb] *svād-*, which belongs to the *lavi* (first) class, becomes *suṇeti*, *suṇenti*, and so forth. In the passive (*kamme*), it is *sūyati*, *sūyare*, *sūyanti*, and so forth.
This is the method for *svād-*.
In the detailed explanation of that [section], from *tan* onwards:
when *la* follows the roots beginning with *tan*, *o* is substituted—thus, *tanoti*, *tanonti*, and so forth. In the group beginning with *par*.
In the case of the substitute *o* for the suffixes *tan*,
*tana*, and *ta*, when followed by the six subsequent suffixes, *u* is substituted [for *o*] in the sense of the object (kamma), as in *tanute*, *tatvante*, and so forth; or it is optional.
The suffix *ta* becomes *ā*, *vā*, *kye*, *tāyati*, *taññāti*, *tāyare*, *tāyanti*, *taññare*, or *taññanti*;
thus ends the method for *tanādi*.
The root *vūra* means "theft."

The suffix *ṇi* follows roots beginning with *cur* when expressing their own meaning; it is applied extensively in the sense of the action itself. For example: *corayati*, *corati*, *corayare*, *corayanti*, *corente*, and so forth. In the passive sense (*kamma*): *coriyati*, *corīyare*, *corīyanti*, and so forth.
The method for the *cur*-class roots begins with "tyādayo" (and so on).
Having completed this grammatical treatise for the benefit of others, may this world,
by means of that merit, attain the state of the deathless through a pure aspiration characterized by perfectly purified virtues.
In the delightful city of Anurādhapura,
he who dwells like a lotus, whose pure lineage is the banner of the wise,
and who is honored by the Saṅgha, causes this to be made with sandalwood.
By one who honors the Tathāgata through the practice of the path, being endowed with faith,
and by means of the fires of constant and unbroken austerity, having scorched all evil deeds,
[he is purified] by the golden vessel of the essence of the lion called the True Dhamma.
By the wise Elder, who was skilled in discerning the various doctrines and diverse views of opposing disputants,
who was compassionate toward new students, who had mastered the succession of the teachers’ traditions,
and who was protected by the cage of his teacher’s feet— he [composed this work] concerning grammar, the seven cases, and so forth.
Thus it is said that the son of Moggallāna was well-trained and easy to instruct; he,
named Piyadassi, became a wise ascetic who had attained happiness,
speaking only what was spoken by his own consort Upabhoginī.
By the maternal uncle named Kappina,
who was tranquil and peerless as a tilaka tree, and who served the mountain-river that flows through the forest of his firm breasts— the wife of the Elder Mahāvihāra.
The establishment of the words is completed.
